docs.title: voles
docs.text:
Collocation-method solvers for Volterra integral and integro-differential equations (VIEs/VIDEs), based on:

Brunner H. Collocation Methods for Volterra Integral and Related Functional Differential Equations. Cambridge University Press; 2004.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
Equation Solver \(g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vie1 \(y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vie2 \(y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vide

Each takes its inputs either as arrays of samples on a uniform grid (dt=), the fastest path for sampled data, or as callables on a mesh you choose (mesh=), which also handles weakly singular kernels. Both return a VolterraSolution. The rules are on the Conventions page.

For a kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=..., t_end=..., n_intervals=..., order=...) builds a Brunner-graded mesh, and declaring the exponent with kernel_singularity={0.0: alpha} switches the singular blocks to fast deterministic Gauss–Jacobi quadrature. Collocation nodes for callable inputs can be given via coll_nodes, with gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes and lobatto_nodes for the classical families.

Upgrading from 0.10? See Migration from 0.10.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install voles[full]

This gives you the fully-capable package, so everything just works out of the box. Pre-built wheels are provided for Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon), and Windows x64. The D extension is bundled in the wheel and requires no extra tooling. Intel Macs are no longer supported as of 0.3.2; users can pin to volterra-equation-solvers==0.3.1 or build from source (see CONTRIBUTING.md).

Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10, numpy, scipy

If you have trouble installing a dependency, you can use a slimmer install instead. numba and scipy are only needed for some features (see below), so any of these will still give you a working package:

pip install voles          # core: numpy + scipy (no numba)
pip install voles --no-deps && pip install numpy   # leanest: numpy only, no scipy or numba

What the optional pieces buy you: - scipy (core dependency) — required for callable inputs and for VolterraSolution.to_ppoly(). - numba (added by [full]) — only needed for sampled inputs with quadrature="collocation" and a collocation setting not compiled into the D extension; the default product quadrature needs neither.

To build from source (e.g. on an unsupported platform), see CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Mathematical derivations
docs.text:
The docs/ directory contains worked derivations of the analytic solutions used in the test suite:

File Contents scalar_solutions.pdf Derivations for all six scalar test cases (VIE-1, VIE-2, VIDE) coupled_vector_solutions.pdf Derivations for the coupled 2×2 vector test cases, constructed via a similarity transform

LaTeX source files are provided alongside the PDFs.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import voles

# y(t) = sin(t) satisfies this VIE-2
dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 9.05, dt)
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt)
print(sol.y[:3], sol(0.123))

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Mean wall-clock execution time, measured on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-22.04 runner (2-core x86_64 VM on an Intel Xeon 8370C, 2.8 GHz base / 3.5 GHz boost). Mean time is averaged over a variable number of calibrated rounds (from ~3 for large inputs up to ~6000 for small inputs). A dash (—) marks sizes a row is not benchmarked at (to keep the CI job fast).

These tables are regenerated automatically by the benchmark CI job on pushes to main that touch code (docs-only pushes are skipped), and this page is redeployed with the fresh numbers. An interactive history of the same measurements is published at the benchmark dashboard.

For the asymptotic complexity (which is what stays fixed as the implementation evolves), see the Benchmarks section of the README.

docs.title: Sampled inputs
docs.text:
Mean time in milliseconds with sampled inputs (arrays, dt=), by input length \(N\) (number of samples). These rows use quadrature="collocation", the compiled path:

Solver \ N 500 1000 2000 4000 8000 16000 32000 VIE-1 0.20 0.25 0.35 0.51 0.87 1.63 3.23 VIE-2 0.20 0.29 0.47 0.84 1.64 3.38 7.08 VIDE 0.24 0.35 0.59 1.04 2.03 4.21 8.73 VIE-2 (Numba fallback) 1.08 3.08 10.2 36.4 139 — — VIE-1 (d=2) 0.36 0.50 0.78 1.28 2.26 4.46 8.91 VIE-2 (d=2) 0.36 0.58 1.07 2.09 4.32 9.10 18.9 VIDE (d=2) 0.44 0.73 1.35 2.64 6.34 11.6 24.6 VIE-2 (d=8) 3.10 6.12 12.6 26.8 55.5 — — VIDE (d=8) 4.17 8.23 16.9 45.7 74.2 — — VIE-2 (d=16) 14.4 36.1 69.3 144 — — —

Notes on the rows:

  • VIE-1 with continuous=True is not shown separately: its timings are indistinguishable from the default (discontinuous) VIE-1 rows.
  • d=8 is the largest compile-time-specialized dimension in the D extension; d=16 exercises the runtime-dimension path (LAPACK, or the pure-D LU fallback used on the CI runner). Cost grows as \(d^2\) either way.
  • Numba fallback: scalar equations with a collocation setting that is not compiled into the D extension fall back to a Numba JIT solver. Every setting with divs ≤ 4 is compiled, so this row uses coll_setting=(5, [0, 3, 5]) — a 3-node rule comparable to the default — whose mesh intervals are 25 fine steps wide instead of 4. The fallback therefore takes ~6× fewer (larger) steps at equal \(N\) than the D rows above, and is still one to two orders of magnitude slower: its history sum is quadratic in the number of mesh intervals, while the D extension uses a blocked-FFT scheme. The one-time JIT compilation cost (seconds, on first call in a fresh environment) is excluded from the timings via a warmup round.

docs.title: Callable inputs
docs.text:
With callable inputs (mesh=) the solvers integrate the kernel numerically (Python + adaptive quadrature), so they are benchmarked on much smaller problems, sized by the number of mesh intervals \(M\) (each carrying len(coll_nodes) collocation nodes). The smooth rows use uniform meshes, on which the weights are assembled from one row (Toeplitz structure). The weakly singular row uses an Abel kernel \(K(u) = u^{-1/2}\) on a graded mesh, with the singularity declared by location only (adaptive quadrature):

Solver \ M 25 50 100 200 VIE-1 1.38 1.73 2.46 4.55 VIE-2 1.38 1.79 2.63 5.11 VIE-2 (vector, d=3) 1.64 2.20 3.47 8.56 VIDE 2.06 2.86 4.47 9.13 VIE-2 (weakly singular) 185 440 1157 3425

docs.title: Two ways to give the inputs
docs.text:
Each solver accepts the kernel and the other input functions in one of two forms, chosen by their types (see Conventions for the full rules):

  • Arrays of samples at t = 0, dt, 2·dt, …, with the spacing given as dt. The kernel array holds K(u) at the lags u = 0, dt, …; the convolution lag is u = t − s. The solver builds a uniform mesh from the samples. The collocation nodes sit on samples and are chosen with coll_setting=(divs, choices), meaning nodes at choices / divs within each interval. By default the integrals use product quadrature, which works for every setting; see Product integration.
  • Callables kernel(u), g(t), a(t), with the mesh breakpoints given as mesh= (a 1-D array from 0 to T). Resolution is set by the mesh, which need not be uniform; the nodes are floats, coll_nodes=.

Every solver returns a VolterraSolution: sol.t and sol.y are the solution on the input grid (the sample times, or the mesh breakpoints), and sol(t) evaluates it anywhere in [0, T].

docs.title: solve_vie1
docs.text:
Solves \(g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(0, 3.005, dt)            # 301 samples
g = np.sin(t)                          # g(0) must be 0 for a first-kind equation

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(t), g=g, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - (np.cos(t) - np.sin(t)))):.1e}")

The default nodes for VIE-1 are (3, [1, 2, 3]), so coll_setting could be left out here. Node sets for which the first-kind method diverges are rejected. The default mesh is 3² = 9 samples wide, wider than for the other two equations, because a first-kind equation amplifies noise in g by about the inverse of the mesh width; see Conventions.

docs.title: solve_vie2
docs.text:
Solves \(y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 4.55, dt)             # 91 samples
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt, coll_setting=3)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.1e}")

coll_setting=3 is short for (3, [0, 1, 2, 3]): every point the method admits.

docs.title: solve_vide
docs.text:
Solves \(y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(0, 0.91, dt)             # 91 samples
a = 1.0 / (1.0 + t**2)
g = (np.cos(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))
     - np.sin(t) / (1.0 + t**2))

sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=a, g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.1e}")

docs.title: Using the solution
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 4.55, dt)
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt)

sol(0.42)                              # a float: anywhere in [0, T]
sol(np.linspace(0, 4.5, 200))          # an array
sol(5.0)                               # nan: outside [0, T]
sol.to_ppoly().derivative()(0.42)      # y'(0.42), through scipy's PPoly
print(sol)

See Working with the solution for the collocation data, the coefficients and the values at breakpoints.

docs.title: Callable inputs
docs.text:
The same problem with callables, on a mesh you choose:

import numpy as np
import voles

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u),
                       g=lambda t: np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t)),
                       mesh=np.linspace(0, 4.5, 91))
print(sol(0.37), np.sin(0.37))

For a weakly singular kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\) (e.g. Abel-type), declare the singularity and use optimal_graded_mesh to recover the full collocation convergence order. With the exponent known, the dict form kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5} switches the singular blocks from adaptive quadrature to much faster deterministic Gauss–Jacobi rules (with an automatic fallback if the declared exponent turns out to be wrong):

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: u**-0.5
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t        # exact y(t) = sqrt(t)

nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=30, order=len(nodes))
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes,
                       kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol(tt) - np.sqrt(tt))):.1e}")

See Callable inputs and arbitrary meshes for more, including vector- and matrix-valued problems.

docs.title: Collocation node helpers
docs.text: Node sets for the coll_nodes parameter (callable inputs). Positions are floats in [0, 1]; these helpers build the classical families. For sampled inputs the nodes must sit on samples and are given as integers through coll_setting; see Conventions.

docs.title: gauss_legendre_nodes
docs.text:
gauss_legendre_nodes(p)

Return the p Gauss-Legendre collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\).

These interior nodes (none at 0 or 1) give the maximal collocation order. For a VIDE the solution superconverges to order \(2p\) at the mesh points. For VIE-2 the collocation solution itself does not: at an interior breakpoint the mean of its one-sided limits (the default of VolterraSolution) gains one order for \(p = 3\) (see the Conventions page, "Values at breakpoints"). For VIE-1 (first kind) Gauss nodes, being symmetric about \(1/2\), have amplification factor \(\rho_p = (-1)^p\): odd \(p\) keeps the full order \(p\), even \(p\) costs one order (see voles.solve_vie1, Notes). radau_iia_nodes have the full order for every \(p\).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes (the order of the collocation method), p >= 1.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \((0, 1)\), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(2)
array([0.21132487, 0.78867513])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def gauss_legendre_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Gauss-Legendre collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$.

    These interior nodes (none at 0 or 1) give the maximal collocation order.
    For a **VIDE** the solution superconverges to order $2p$ at the mesh
    points. For **VIE-2** the collocation solution itself does not: at an
    interior breakpoint the mean of its one-sided limits (the default of
    `VolterraSolution`) gains one order for $p = 3$ (see the Conventions
    page, "Values at breakpoints"). For **VIE-1** (first kind) Gauss nodes,
    being symmetric about $1/2$, have amplification factor
    $\rho_p = (-1)^p$: odd $p$ keeps the full order $p$, even $p$ costs one
    order (see `voles.solve_vie1`, Notes). ``radau_iia_nodes`` have the full
    order for every $p$.

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes (the order of the collocation method), ``p >= 1``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $(0, 1)$, sorted ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(2)
    array([0.21132487, 0.78867513])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=1, name="Gauss-Legendre")
    x, _ = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(p)
    return np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))

docs.title: radau_iia_nodes
docs.text:
radau_iia_nodes(p)

Return the p Radau IIA collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\).

The Radau IIA nodes include the right endpoint (1.0) and exclude 0. They give mesh-point superconvergence of order \(2p - 1\): for a VIDE directly, and for VIE-2 in the left limit at each breakpoint, which is the collocation value at the last node (sol(t, at_breakpoints="left"); the default mean has order \(p\)). The right-endpoint node also makes them a common choice for stiff VIDEs. For the default (discontinuous) VIE-1 method they are the recommended family: the endpoint node makes the amplification factor \(\rho_p = 0\), giving the full order \(p\) for every \(p\) (Gauss-Legendre nodes have \(\rho_p = (-1)^p\) and lose an order for even \(p\)). They do not suit continuous=True, where \(|\rho_{p-1}| = p\) and the method diverges for \(p \ge 2\) (see voles.solve_vie1, Notes).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes, p >= 1.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \((0, 1]\) (the last is exactly 1.0), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.radau_iia_nodes(2)
array([0.33333333, 1.        ])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def radau_iia_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Radau IIA collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$.

    The Radau IIA nodes include the right endpoint (``1.0``) and exclude 0.
    They give mesh-point superconvergence of order $2p - 1$: for a **VIDE**
    directly, and for **VIE-2** in the left limit at each breakpoint, which
    is the collocation value at the last node
    (``sol(t, at_breakpoints="left")``; the default mean has order $p$). The
    right-endpoint node also makes them a common choice for stiff VIDEs. For
    the default (discontinuous) **VIE-1** method they are the recommended
    family: the endpoint node makes the amplification factor $\rho_p = 0$,
    giving the full order $p$ for every $p$ (Gauss-Legendre nodes have
    $\rho_p = (-1)^p$ and lose an order for even $p$). They do not suit
    ``continuous=True``, where $|\rho_{p-1}| = p$ and the method diverges for
    $p \ge 2$ (see `voles.solve_vie1`, Notes).

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes, ``p >= 1``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $(0, 1]$ (the last is exactly ``1.0``), sorted
        ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.radau_iia_nodes(2)
    array([0.33333333, 1.        ])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=1, name="Radau IIA")
    # On [-1, 1] the Radau IIA nodes are the roots of P_{p-1}(x) - P_p(x); one
    # of those roots is +1. Map the roots to [0, 1].
    c = np.zeros(p + 1)
    c[p - 1] += 1.0
    c[p] -= 1.0
    # legroots may return a complex-dtype array (tiny imaginary parts from the
    # companion-matrix eigensolver) on some numpy/LAPACK versions; these nodes
    # are mathematically real, so take the real part.
    x = np.polynomial.legendre.legroots(c).real
    nodes = np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))
    nodes[-1] = 1.0  # pin the endpoint exactly
    return nodes

docs.title: lobatto_nodes
docs.text:
lobatto_nodes(p)

Return the p Gauss-Lobatto collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\) (p >= 2).

The Lobatto nodes include both endpoints (0.0 and 1.0) and have local order \(2p - 2\). Because 0 is included they suit VIE-2 and VIDE but not VIE-1, which forbids a node at \(t = 0\).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes, p >= 2.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \([0, 1]\) (the first is 0.0 and the last 1.0), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.lobatto_nodes(3)
array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def lobatto_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Gauss-Lobatto collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$ (``p >= 2``).

    The Lobatto nodes include both endpoints (``0.0`` and ``1.0``) and have
    local order $2p - 2$. Because 0 is included they suit VIE-2 and VIDE but
    **not** VIE-1, which forbids a node at $t = 0$.

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes, ``p >= 2``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $[0, 1]$ (the first is ``0.0`` and the last ``1.0``),
        sorted ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.lobatto_nodes(3)
    array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=2, name="Lobatto")
    if p == 2:
        interior = np.array([])
    else:
        # The interior Lobatto nodes are the roots of P'_{p-1}.
        c = np.zeros(p)
        c[p - 1] = 1.0
        # .real: legroots may return complex dtype (see radau_iia_nodes); these
        # interior nodes are mathematically real.
        interior = np.polynomial.legendre.legroots(
            np.polynomial.legendre.legder(c)).real
    x = np.concatenate(([-1.0], interior, [1.0]))
    nodes = np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))
    nodes[0] = 0.0   # pin the endpoints exactly
    nodes[-1] = 1.0
    return nodes

docs.title: Compiled collocation settings
docs.text: With the default quadrature="product" the solvers accept every valid coll_setting. With quadrature="collocation" they run routines compiled into the extension for a fixed list of settings (divs ≤ 4 in current builds); any other setting runs on the optional numba fallback (scalar problems only, with a PerformanceWarning) or raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Deprecated 0.10 solvers
docs.text: These six functions are the 0.10 API. They still work in 0.11 and return what they returned in 0.10, but each call issues a DeprecationWarning naming the equivalent new call, and they are removed in 1.0. A few invalid inputs are handled differently from 0.10 (diagnostics are warnings, wrong types raise TypeError, non-finite data is rejected). See Migration from 0.10.

docs.title: solve_VIE_1
docs.text:
solve_VIE_1(*, kernel_values, g_values=None, soln_init_value=None, time_step=1.0, coll_divs=None, coll_choices=None, return_function=False, return_polys=None, force_continuous=False, show_warnings=True, quadrature='product', mesh_samples=None, kernel_interp_degree=None)

Solve a Volterra integral equation of the first kind.

Deprecated since 0.11; removed in 1.0. Use voles.solve_vie1 instead; each call warns with the equivalent 1.0 call.

Finds \(y(t)\) satisfying

\[g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\]

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kernel_values array_like of shape (N,) or (N, d, d)

Values of \(K(s)\) at times \(s = 0, h, 2h, \ldots, (N-1)h\), where \(h\) is time_step. Pass a 1-D array for scalar equations or a 3-D array of shape (N, d, d) for \(d\)-dimensional vector equations.

required g_values array_like of shape (N,) or (N, d) or (N, d, m)

Right-hand side \(g(t)\) sampled at the same times as kernel_values. For matrix-valued equations pass shape (N, d, m) to solve \(m\) right-hand sides simultaneously. Defaults to zero.

None soln_init_value float or array_like of shape (d,) or (d, m)

Initial value \(y(0)\) imposed when force_continuous=True. Has no effect when force_continuous=False (default). Required when force_continuous=True. It must be the value the equation implies: differentiating at \(t = 0\) gives \(g'(0) = K(0)\,y(0)\). Any other value gives a wrong solution on the whole interval, not only near \(t = 0\), and is not detected. If \(y(0)\) is not known independently, use the default method, or estimate it by solving with force_continuous=False, return_function=True and evaluating the solution at \(t = 0\) (the continuous solve is then more accurate than the default method but falls short of its full order).

None time_step float

Spacing \(h\) between consecutive sample times. Must be positive. Default is 1.0.

1.0 coll_divs int

Number of collocation sub-intervals per mesh interval. Must be a positive integer. Given alone, the nodes are all its sub-interval points, coll_choices = [1, ..., coll_divs] (the right endpoint included, so \(\rho_m = 0\) and the method has its full order); given neither, the setting is coll_divs=3, coll_choices=[1, 2, 3].

None coll_choices list of int

Indices selecting the collocation nodes within each sub-interval. Each entry \(k\) corresponds to the node \(k / c\) where \(c\) = coll_divs, placed in \((0, 1]\); zero is excluded. Entries must be distinct integers in \(\{1, \ldots, \text{coll\_divs}\}\). Given alone, coll_divs is the largest entry.

None return_function bool

If True, also return a callable solution object as the second element of a tuple (see Returns). Default is False.

False return_polys bool

Deprecated alias for return_function; passing it emits a DeprecationWarning.

None force_continuous bool

If True, use the continuous collocation method (Brunner's \(S_m^{(0)}\)): on each mesh interval the solution is a polynomial of degree \(m\) (one more than the default) that is continuous across mesh points, starting from soln_init_value at \(t = 0\). Requires the last collocation node to be the right endpoint of the mesh interval (max(coll_choices) == coll_divs) and a node set with \(|\rho_{m-1}| \le 1\) (see Notes). Converges with order \(m + 1\) when \(-1 \le \rho_{m-1} < 1\) and with order \(m\) when \(\rho_{m-1} = 1\), versus order \(m\) for the default discontinuous method with the same nodes. Default is False.

False show_warnings bool

    but not at the samples inside the final interval.

    interpolated kernel; the kernel-perturbation error is of order
    $\delta^{p+1}$ for interpolation degree $p$, the mesh is ``mesh_samples``
    samples wide (with the same final-interval treatment of leftover samples
    as above, so any length of at least ``mesh_samples + 1`` is accepted),
    and the lag structure of the blocks lets the FFT-accelerated history of
    the D extension be used.

    The solver dispatches at runtime to a D-extension routine specialised for
    the given collocation setting. For scalar equations, settings not compiled
    into the extension fall back to a Numba-JIT implementation (requires the
    ``numba`` optional dependency), with a `voles.PerformanceWarning`. For vector equations only the compiled settings are supported. The
    compiled settings are listed in ``fast_coll_settings_VIDE``.

    ----------
    .. [1] Brunner, H. *Collocation Methods for Volterra Integral and Related
       Functional Differential Equations.* Cambridge University Press, 2004.
       Chapter 3, pp. 160–167.

    _deprecated_call(solve_VIDE, kwargs)
    return _sampled.vide(**kwargs)

\(y(0)\). Required only when force_continuous=True; ignored otherwise. A warning is emitted if a value is passed when it has no effect. For a matrix-valued problem with force_continuous=True it must have shape \((d, m)\). It must be the value the equation implies: differentiating at \(t = 0\) gives \(g'(0) = K(0)\,y(0)\). Any other value gives a wrong solution on the whole interval, not only near \(t = 0\), and is not detected. (soln_values, y_callable) : tuple

When return_function=True; y_callable as in function_solve_VIE_2.

As for function_solve_VIE_2; additionally ValueError for non-convergent node sets (see Notes), zero in coll_choices / coll_nodes, force_continuous without \(c_m = 1\), force_continuous without soln_init_value, or a non-finite soln_init_value; TypeError for a force_continuous that is not a bool.

The equation forces \(g(0) = 0\); for \(g(0) \ne 0\) there is no bounded solution, and a voles.AccuracyWarning is emitted.

Whether a given node set yields a convergent method depends on the nodes (Brunner 2004, smooth-kernel chapter). For a smooth kernel with \(|K(t, t)| \ge k_0 > 0\), writing \(c_1 < \dots < c_m\) for the nodes:

The amplification criteria do not apply to weakly-singular kernels (where \(|K(t, t)|\) is unbounded), so they are skipped when kernel_singularity is given and convergence is then the caller's responsibility. The \(c_m = 1\) requirement of force_continuous is not part of these criteria -- it is structural and always enforced.

These theorems are proved for a uniform mesh. The amplification factors \(\rho\) depend only on the nodes, so the conditions carry over to quasi-uniform meshes (all interval widths within fixed constant multiples of each other). They are not guaranteed on strongly graded meshes -- e.g. the geometric refinement of optimal_graded_mesh, where the smallest interval shrinks far faster than the largest -- but such meshes normally accompany a declared kernel_singularity, for which the check is already skipped.

function_solve_VIE_2(*, kernel, g=None, mesh_breakpoints, coll_divs=None, coll_choices=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, return_function=False, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True, show_warnings=True)

Solve the scalar Volterra integral equation of the second kind

Deprecated since 0.11; removed in 1.0. Use voles.solve_vie2 instead; each call warns with the equivalent 1.0 call.

\[y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\]

with callable kernel and right-hand side, on an arbitrary mesh.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kernel callable

kernel(u) returns \(K(u)\) for scalar \(u > 0\): a scalar for scalar equations, or a square \((d, d)\) matrix for \(d\)-dimensional vector and matrix-valued equations. For the fastest weight assembly, make kernel accept a 1-D array of u values and return the matching (n,) or (n, d, d) array (e.g. np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A) rather than np.exp(-u) * A): the smooth blocks of a whole mesh row are then evaluated in one call. A kernel that only accepts scalars still works, through a per-point path that can be several times slower.

required g callable

g(t) returns the forcing term \(g(t)\). Defaults to zero. Return a scalar for scalar equations, a \((d,)\) array for vector equations, or a \((d, m)\) array to solve \(m\) right-hand sides simultaneously (the matrix-valued case). A 2-D return signals the matrix case; matrix-valued problems require a \((d, d)\) matrix kernel.

None mesh_breakpoints array_like

Strictly increasing 1-D array starting at 0. Defines the integration intervals directly.

required coll_divs int, list of int

Collocation node positions: nodes lie at coll_choices[k] / coll_divs in each interval. Unlike the array- based solvers, coll_divs does not sub-divide intervals. coll_divs alone selects every admissible point of the subdivision, coll_choices = [0, ..., coll_divs]; coll_choices alone sets coll_divs to its largest entry; neither gives coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2]. Mutually exclusive with coll_nodes.

None coll_choices int, list of int

Collocation node positions: nodes lie at coll_choices[k] / coll_divs in each interval. Unlike the array- based solvers, coll_divs does not sub-divide intervals. coll_divs alone selects every admissible point of the subdivision, coll_choices = [0, ..., coll_divs]; coll_choices alone sets coll_divs to its largest entry; neither gives coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2]. Mutually exclusive with coll_nodes.

None coll_nodes array_like

Collocation node positions given directly as floats in \([0, 1]\), for node sets that are not rational multiples of \(1/c\) (e.g. Gauss-Legendre or Radau IIA points; see gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes, lobatto_nodes). Mutually exclusive with coll_divs/coll_choices. Convergence of the chosen node set is the caller's responsibility.

None kernel_singularity None, float, list of float, dict, or callable

Declare the singularity structure of the kernel.

  • None: kernel is smooth everywhere.
  • float or list of float: convolution-style singularity locations (in \(u = t - s\)); e.g. 0.0 for \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\). Blocks touching a location are integrated adaptively.
  • dict {location: alpha}: like the list form, but a non-None alpha additionally declares the power law \(K(u) \sim |u - u_0|^{-\alpha}\) (with \(0 < \alpha < 1\); use {0.0: 0.5} for an Abel kernel \(u^{-1/2}\)). Blocks touching such a location are integrated by deterministic fixed-order Gauss-Jacobi rules with the singular factor absorbed into the weight: typically much faster and more accurate than adaptive quadrature, and -- being deterministic -- reusable across the uniform-mesh Toeplitz assembly under the default strict policy, so the singular build runs at smooth-kernel speed with no reuse_adaptive_blocks flag needed. Each Jacobi block passes the same two-order acceptance check as the smooth path; a failing basis function (wrong declared alpha, or extra structure like a log factor) falls back to the adaptive treatment automatically. alpha=None keeps a location fully adaptive.
  • callable f(t) -> list[float]: returns the singular \(s\)-locations for collocation point \(t\). Forward-compatible with non-convolution \(K(s, t)\).

Locations may be Python floats/ints, NumPy scalars, or 0-d arrays; booleans are rejected with a TypeError (True would silently mean location 1.0). An empty list/tuple/dict declares nothing and behaves exactly like None. The kernel's return value exactly at a declared singular point is never used (it is masked out of the quadrature), so returning 0, inf, or a clamped value there are all equivalent.

None return_function bool

If True, also return a callable solution wrapper.

False reuse_adaptive_blocks bool

On a uniform mesh with a convolution kernel the weight tensor is Toeplitz and is assembled from one integrated row. Blocks evaluated by deterministic fixed-order quadrature are always reused across rows. With the default True, blocks touching a declared singularity that need adaptive quadrature are reused too, computed once at a tightened tolerance: the singular-kernel build cost is about an order of magnitude lower than re-evaluating them per row. False re-evaluates those blocks for every row, which reproduces the general (non-Toeplitz) assembly to rounding level at an \(O(M)\) adaptive-quadrature cost; the two differ by at most the adaptive quadrature's own tolerance (scalar problems \(\sim10^{-8}\), typically \(\sim10^{-9}\); vector/matrix and complex problems, which integrate via scipy.integrate.quad_vec, up to \(\sim10^{-7}\)), far below discretization error in practice. No effect on non-uniform meshes or on kernels with no declared kernel_singularity. scipy IntegrationWarnings raised by the deliberately tightened reuse quadratures are suppressed (the best-obtainable value is what reuse wants); default-tolerance quadratures still warn as usual.

True show_warnings bool

If True (default), emit a voles.AccuracyWarning when a kernel_singularity is declared on a mesh that looks uniform (suggesting optimal_graded_mesh), and a voles.VolesWarning when a declared location lies outside \([0, T]\). False emits nothing; the standard warnings filters work as well.

True

Returns:

Name Type Description soln_values ndarray

Solution values at collocation nodes, where M is the number of intervals and p is the number of collocation nodes per interval (len(coll_choices) or len(coll_nodes)). Shape (M, p) for scalar equations, (M, p, d) for vector equations, and (M, p, d, m) for matrix-valued equations.

(soln_values, y_callable) : tuple

When return_function=True. y_callable(t) evaluates the piecewise polynomial at any time t in the mesh (NaN outside it), returning a scalar / (d,) / (d, m) value for scalar t (with a leading time axis for array t).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

For invalid meshes, collocation settings, kernel_singularity declarations (out-of-range alpha), non-finite weight-tensor entries, a g returning NaN or infinity at a collocation time, kernel dimension or node count past the compiled limits, or matrix input with zero columns.

TypeError

If kernel or g is not callable; for a coll_divs or coll_choices entry that is not an integer (floats are rejected, not truncated); for a kernel_singularity location that is a bool or not a number; or for a flag (return_function, reuse_adaptive_blocks, show_warnings) that is not a bool.

LinAlgError

If a collocation system is singular or nearly singular (e.g. a zero kernel).

ImportError

If scipy is not installed.

Notes

See the module docstring for the mesh-convention difference from the array-based solvers.

Matrix-valued problems share the kernel weight tensor across all \(m\) right-hand sides (it is built once), so they are substantially cheaper than \(m\) separate calls. The \(m\) columns are solved in threads (capped at the CPU count).

          treatment automatically. ``alpha=None`` keeps a location fully
          adaptive.
        - callable ``f(t) -> list[float]``: returns the singular $s$-locations
          for collocation point $t$. Forward-compatible with non-convolution
          $K(s, t)$.

        Locations may be Python floats/ints, NumPy scalars, or 0-d arrays;
        booleans are rejected with a ``TypeError`` (``True`` would silently
        mean location 1.0). An empty list/tuple/dict declares nothing and
        behaves exactly like ``None``. The kernel's return value exactly *at*
        a declared singular point is never used (it is masked out of the
        quadrature), so returning 0, ``inf``, or a clamped value there are
        all equivalent.
    return_function : bool, optional
        If True, also return a callable solution wrapper.
    reuse_adaptive_blocks : bool, optional
        On a uniform mesh with a convolution kernel the weight tensor is
        Toeplitz and is assembled from one integrated row. Blocks evaluated
        by deterministic fixed-order quadrature are always reused across
        rows. With the default ``True``, blocks touching a declared
        singularity that need adaptive quadrature are reused too, computed
        once at a tightened tolerance: the singular-kernel build cost is
        about an order of magnitude lower than re-evaluating them per row.
        ``False`` re-evaluates those blocks for every row, which reproduces
        the general (non-Toeplitz) assembly to rounding level at an $O(M)$
        adaptive-quadrature cost; the two differ by at most the adaptive
        quadrature's own tolerance (scalar problems $\sim10^{-8}$, typically
        $\sim10^{-9}$; vector/matrix and complex problems, which integrate
        via ``scipy.integrate.quad_vec``, up to $\sim10^{-7}$), far below
        discretization error in practice. No effect on non-uniform meshes
        or on kernels with no declared ``kernel_singularity``. scipy
        ``IntegrationWarning``s raised by the deliberately tightened reuse
        quadratures are suppressed (the best-obtainable value is what reuse
        wants); default-tolerance quadratures still warn as usual.
    show_warnings : bool, optional
        If True (default), emit a `voles.AccuracyWarning` when a
        ``kernel_singularity`` is declared on a mesh that looks uniform
        (suggesting ``optimal_graded_mesh``), and a `voles.VolesWarning` when
        a declared location lies outside $[0, T]$. ``False`` emits nothing;
        the standard `warnings` filters work as well.

    Returns
    -------
    soln_values : ndarray
        Solution values at collocation nodes, where M is the number of
        intervals and p is the number of collocation nodes per interval
        (``len(coll_choices)`` or ``len(coll_nodes)``). Shape ``(M, p)`` for
        scalar equations, ``(M, p, d)`` for vector equations, and
        ``(M, p, d, m)`` for matrix-valued equations.
    (soln_values, y_callable) : tuple
        When ``return_function=True``. ``y_callable(t)`` evaluates the
        piecewise polynomial at any time t in the mesh (NaN outside it), returning a scalar / ``(d,)`` /
        ``(d, m)`` value for scalar t (with a leading time axis for array t).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For invalid meshes, collocation settings, ``kernel_singularity``
        declarations (out-of-range ``alpha``), non-finite weight-tensor
        entries, a ``g`` returning NaN or infinity at a collocation time,
        kernel dimension or node count past the compiled limits, or matrix
        input with zero columns.
    TypeError
        If ``kernel`` or ``g`` is not callable; for a ``coll_divs`` or
        ``coll_choices`` entry that is not an integer (floats are rejected,
        not truncated); for a ``kernel_singularity`` location that is a bool
        or not a number; or for a flag (``return_function``,
        ``reuse_adaptive_blocks``, ``show_warnings``) that is not a bool.
    numpy.linalg.LinAlgError
        If a collocation system is singular or nearly singular (e.g. a zero
        kernel).
    ImportError
        If scipy is not installed.

    Notes
    -----
    See the module docstring for the mesh-convention difference from the
    array-based solvers.

    Matrix-valued problems share the kernel weight tensor across all $m$
    right-hand sides (it is built once), so they are substantially cheaper than
    $m$ separate calls. The $m$ columns are solved in threads (capped at the
    CPU count).
    """
    kwargs = dict(locals())
    _deprecated_call(function_solve_VIE_2, kwargs)
    return _functional.vie2(**kwargs)

function_solve_VIDE(*, kernel, a=None, g=None, soln_init_value, mesh_breakpoints, coll_divs=None, coll_choices=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, return_function=False, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True, show_warnings=True)

Solve the scalar Volterra integro-differential equation

Deprecated since 0.11; removed in 1.0. Use voles.solve_vide instead; each call warns with the equivalent 1.0 call.

\[y'(t) = a(t)\,y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds,\quad y(0) = y_0\]

with callable inputs on an arbitrary mesh.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kernel callable

kernel(u) returns \(K(u)\): a scalar, or a \((d, d)\) matrix for vector and matrix-valued equations. For the fastest weight assembly, make kernel accept a 1-D array of u values and return the matching (n,) or (n, d, d) array (e.g. np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A) rather than np.exp(-u) * A): the smooth blocks of a whole mesh row are then evaluated in one call. A kernel that only accepts scalars still works, through a per-point path that can be several times slower.

required a callable

a(t) returns the coefficient \(a(t)\) (a scalar, or a \((d, d)\) matrix for vector/matrix equations). Defaults to zero. a does not depend on the right-hand side, so it is sampled once in the matrix case.

None g callable

g(t) returns the forcing term: scalar, \((d,)\), or \((d, m)\) for the matrix-valued case. Defaults to zero.

None soln_init_value float or array_like

\(y(0)\). Required. A scalar/(d,) value gives the scalar/vector case; a \((d, m)\) array selects the matrix-valued case (\(m\) right-hand sides).

required mesh_breakpoints array_like

Strictly-increasing 1-D array starting at 0.

required coll_divs int, list of int

Collocation node positions; see function_solve_VIE_2 for the convention (differs from the array-based solvers). coll_divs alone selects coll_choices = [0, ..., coll_divs], coll_choices alone sets coll_divs to its largest entry, and neither gives coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2]. Mutually exclusive with coll_nodes.

None coll_choices int, list of int

Collocation node positions; see function_solve_VIE_2 for the convention (differs from the array-based solvers). coll_divs alone selects coll_choices = [0, ..., coll_divs], coll_choices alone sets coll_divs to its largest entry, and neither gives coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2]. Mutually exclusive with coll_nodes.

None coll_nodes array_like

Collocation node positions given directly as floats in \([0, 1]\); see function_solve_VIE_2. Mutually exclusive with coll_divs/coll_choices.

None kernel_singularity None, float, list of float, dict, or callable

Declare integrable singularities, optionally with known power-law exponents (dict form, enabling deterministic Gauss-Jacobi rules); see function_solve_VIE_2.

None return_function bool

If True, also return a callable solution wrapper.

False reuse_adaptive_blocks bool

Reuse the adaptive-quadrature weight blocks across the uniform-mesh Toeplitz assembly; see function_solve_VIE_2.

True show_warnings bool

If True (default), emit the kernel_singularity warnings described in function_solve_VIE_2.

True

Returns:

Name Type Description soln_values ndarray

\(y\) values at collocation nodes. Shape (M, p) (scalar), (M, p, d) (vector), or (M, p, d, m) (matrix-valued), with p the number of collocation nodes per interval.

(soln_values, y_callable) : tuple

When return_function=True.

Raises:

Type Description (ValueError, TypeError, LinAlgError, ImportError)

As for function_solve_VIE_2; additionally TypeError when soln_init_value is omitted or None, and ValueError when its shape is incompatible with the kernel dimension, when it or a(t) is not finite.

Notes

Internally the unknowns are \(y'\) at the collocation nodes; the returned values are \(y\) itself (reconstructed via the antiderivative basis and the tracked boundary values).

def function_solve_VIDE(*, kernel, a=None, g=None, soln_init_value,
                         mesh_breakpoints,
                         coll_divs: int = None, coll_choices: list[int] = None,
                         coll_nodes=None,
                         kernel_singularity=None,
                         return_function: bool = False,
                         reuse_adaptive_blocks: bool = True,
                         show_warnings: bool = True):
    r"""Solve the scalar Volterra integro-differential equation

    **Deprecated since 0.11; removed in 1.0.** Use `voles.solve_vide` instead; each call warns
    with the equivalent 1.0 call.

    $$y'(t) = a(t)\,y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds,\quad y(0) = y_0$$

    with callable inputs on an arbitrary mesh.

    Parameters
    ----------
    kernel : callable
        ``kernel(u)`` returns $K(u)$: a scalar, or a $(d, d)$ matrix for vector
        and matrix-valued equations.
        For the fastest weight assembly, make ``kernel`` accept a 1-D array
        of ``u`` values and return the matching ``(n,)`` or ``(n, d, d)``
        array (e.g. ``np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A)`` rather than
        ``np.exp(-u) * A``): the smooth blocks of a whole mesh row are then
        evaluated in one call. A kernel that only accepts scalars still
        works, through a per-point path that can be several times slower.
    a : callable, optional
        ``a(t)`` returns the coefficient $a(t)$ (a scalar, or a $(d, d)$ matrix
        for vector/matrix equations). Defaults to zero. ``a`` does not depend on
        the right-hand side, so it is sampled once in the matrix case.
    g : callable, optional
        ``g(t)`` returns the forcing term: scalar, $(d,)$, or $(d, m)$ for the
        matrix-valued case. Defaults to zero.
    soln_init_value : float or array_like
        $y(0)$. Required. A scalar/`(d,)` value gives the scalar/vector case; a
        $(d, m)$ array selects the matrix-valued case ($m$ right-hand sides).
    mesh_breakpoints : array_like
        Strictly-increasing 1-D array starting at 0.
    coll_divs, coll_choices : int, list of int, optional
        Collocation node positions; see ``function_solve_VIE_2`` for the
        convention (differs from the array-based solvers). ``coll_divs``
        alone selects ``coll_choices = [0, ..., coll_divs]``, ``coll_choices``
        alone sets ``coll_divs`` to its largest entry, and neither gives
        ``coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2]``. Mutually exclusive with
        ``coll_nodes``.
    coll_nodes : array_like, optional
        Collocation node positions given directly as floats in $[0, 1]$; see
        ``function_solve_VIE_2``. Mutually exclusive with
        ``coll_divs``/``coll_choices``.
    kernel_singularity : None, float, list of float, dict, or callable
        Declare integrable singularities, optionally with known power-law
        exponents (dict form, enabling deterministic Gauss-Jacobi rules);
        see ``function_solve_VIE_2``.
    return_function : bool, optional
        If True, also return a callable solution wrapper.
    reuse_adaptive_blocks : bool, optional
        Reuse the adaptive-quadrature weight blocks across the uniform-mesh
        Toeplitz assembly; see ``function_solve_VIE_2``.
    show_warnings : bool, optional
        If True (default), emit the ``kernel_singularity`` warnings described
        in ``function_solve_VIE_2``.

    Returns
    -------
    soln_values : ndarray
        $y$ values at collocation nodes. Shape ``(M, p)`` (scalar),
        ``(M, p, d)`` (vector), or ``(M, p, d, m)`` (matrix-valued), with p
        the number of collocation nodes per interval.
    (soln_values, y_callable) : tuple
        When ``return_function=True``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError, TypeError, numpy.linalg.LinAlgError, ImportError
        As for ``function_solve_VIE_2``; additionally ``TypeError`` when
        ``soln_init_value`` is omitted or None, and ``ValueError`` when its
        shape is incompatible with the kernel dimension, when it or ``a(t)``
        is not finite.

    Notes
    -----
    Internally the unknowns are $y'$ at the collocation nodes; the returned
    values are $y$ itself (reconstructed via the antiderivative basis and the
    tracked boundary values).
    """
    kwargs = dict(locals())
    _deprecated_call(function_solve_VIDE, kwargs)
    return _functional.vide(**kwargs)

docs.title: optimal_graded_mesh
docs.text:
optimal_graded_mesh(*, alpha, t_end=None, n_intervals=None, order, T=None, M=None)

Return a graded mesh of n_intervals + 1 breakpoints suitable for a weakly singular convolution kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in [0, 1)\).

Grading: \(t_n = T (n/M)^r\) with \(T\) = t_end, \(M\) = n_intervals and \(r = p / (1 - \alpha)\), where \(p\) = order is the order of the collocation method (the number of collocation nodes per interval). This recovers the optimal convergence order for Abel-type kernels (Brunner 2004, ch. 6). At alpha == 0 the kernel is non-singular and the solution smooth, so a uniform mesh (\(r = 1\)) is returned instead.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default alpha float

Singularity exponent, in \([0, 1)\).

required t_end float

Right endpoint of the mesh (positive).

None n_intervals int

Number of intervals (positive). The returned array has length n_intervals + 1.

None order int

Order of the collocation method (positive). For a matched mesh, pass the number of collocation nodes the solver uses.

required T (float, int)

Deprecated spellings of t_end and n_intervals (0.10); they still work in 0.11, with a DeprecationWarning, and are removed in 1.0.

None M (float, int)

Deprecated spellings of t_end and n_intervals (0.10); they still work in 0.11, with a DeprecationWarning, and are removed in 1.0.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (n_intervals + 1,)

Strictly increasing breakpoints with [0] == 0 and [-1] == t_end.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If alpha is outside \([0, 1)\), t_end is not positive and finite, or n_intervals / order is less than 1.

TypeError

If alpha or t_end is not a real number, n_intervals / order is not an integer, or t_end / n_intervals is missing (or given together with its deprecated spelling).

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=4, order=2)
array([0.        , 0.00390625, 0.0625    , 0.31640625, 1.        ])

Grade for the same order as the solver's collocation method. The solution of \(y(t) = 1 + \int_0^t (t-s)^{-1/2} y(s)\,ds\) is \(\operatorname{erfcx}(-\sqrt{\pi t})\):

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.special import erfcx
>>> nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
>>> mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=60,
...                                  order=len(nodes))
>>> sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: u**-0.5, g=lambda t: np.ones_like(t),
...                        mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
>>> print(f"relative error {abs(sol(1.0) / erfcx(-np.sqrt(np.pi)) - 1):.1e}")
relative error 1.3e-05

def optimal_graded_mesh(*, alpha: float, t_end: Optional[float] = None,
                        n_intervals: Optional[int] = None, order: int,
                        T: Optional[float] = None, M: Optional[int] = None) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return a graded mesh of ``n_intervals + 1`` breakpoints suitable for a
    weakly singular convolution kernel $K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}$,
    $\alpha \in [0, 1)$.

    Grading: $t_n = T (n/M)^r$ with $T$ = ``t_end``, $M$ = ``n_intervals``
    and $r = p / (1 - \alpha)$, where $p$ = ``order`` is the order of the
    collocation method (the number of collocation nodes per interval). This
    recovers the optimal convergence order for Abel-type kernels (Brunner
    2004, ch. 6). At ``alpha == 0`` the kernel is non-singular and the
    solution smooth, so a uniform mesh ($r = 1$) is returned instead.

    Parameters
    ----------
    alpha : float
        Singularity exponent, in $[0, 1)$.
    t_end : float
        Right endpoint of the mesh (positive).
    n_intervals : int
        Number of intervals (positive). The returned array has length
        ``n_intervals + 1``.
    order : int
        Order of the collocation method (positive). For a matched mesh,
        pass the number of collocation nodes the solver uses.
    T, M : float, int
        Deprecated spellings of ``t_end`` and ``n_intervals`` (0.10); they
        still work in 0.11, with a `DeprecationWarning`, and are removed in
        1.0.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (n_intervals + 1,)
        Strictly increasing breakpoints with ``[0] == 0`` and
        ``[-1] == t_end``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``alpha`` is outside $[0, 1)$, ``t_end`` is not positive and
        finite, or ``n_intervals`` / ``order`` is less than 1.
    TypeError
        If ``alpha`` or ``t_end`` is not a real number, ``n_intervals`` /
        ``order`` is not an integer, or ``t_end`` / ``n_intervals`` is
        missing (or given together with its deprecated spelling).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=4, order=2)
    array([0.        , 0.00390625, 0.0625    , 0.31640625, 1.        ])

    Grade for the same order as the solver's collocation method. The
    solution of $y(t) = 1 + \int_0^t (t-s)^{-1/2} y(s)\,ds$ is
    $\operatorname{erfcx}(-\sqrt{\pi t})$:

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from scipy.special import erfcx
    >>> nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
    >>> mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=60,
    ...                                  order=len(nodes))
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: u**-0.5, g=lambda t: np.ones_like(t),
    ...                        mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
    >>> print(f"relative error {abs(sol(1.0) / erfcx(-np.sqrt(np.pi)) - 1):.1e}")
    relative error 1.3e-05
    """
    t_end = _renamed("t_end", t_end, "T", T)
    n_intervals = _renamed("n_intervals", n_intervals, "M", M)
    alpha = _v.real("alpha", alpha)
    if not 0.0 <= alpha < 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"alpha must satisfy 0 <= alpha < 1, got {alpha}")
    t_end = _v.real("t_end", t_end, positive=True,
                    value_msg=f"t_end must be positive and finite, got {t_end}")
    n_intervals = _v.integer("n_intervals", n_intervals, minimum=1,
                             value_msg=f"n_intervals must be a positive integer, got {n_intervals}")
    order = _v.integer("order", order, minimum=1,
                       type_msg=f"order must be a positive integer, got {order!r}",
                       value_msg=f"order must be a positive integer, got {order}")
    p = order
    # At alpha=0 the kernel is non-singular and the solution is smooth, so a
    # uniform mesh (r=1) is optimal; grading would only waste resolution near 0.
    r = p / (1.0 - alpha) if alpha > 0.0 else 1.0
    n = np.arange(n_intervals + 1, dtype=np.float64)
    return t_end * (n / n_intervals) ** r

docs.title: VolterraSolution
docs.text:
The solution of a Volterra equation, as returned by the solvers.

A piecewise polynomial on mesh (continuous or discontinuous at the breakpoints), together with its values on the grid the problem was posed on, the collocation data, and a record of the method. Call it to evaluate the solution anywhere in [0, T].

Users don't construct it; every solver returns one.

Attributes:

Name Type Description t (ndarray, shape(K))

The grid the problem was posed on: the sample times n * dt for sampled inputs, the mesh breakpoints for callable inputs. Read-only.

y (ndarray, shape(K, *shape))

The solution at t. At an interior breakpoint of a discontinuous solution this is the mean of the two one-sided limits, the same value sol(t) gives. Writable; changing it doesn't change the solution.

mesh (ndarray, shape(M + 1))

The breakpoints 0 = t_0 < ... < t_M = T.

node_times (ndarray, shape(M, p))

The collocation times actually used. For sampled inputs the final interval may be longer than the others, and its nodes sit on its own sample grid, so they can differ from mesh[n] + nodes * h_n.

node_values (ndarray, shape(M, p, *shape))

The solution at node_times: the collocation values.

coefficients (ndarray, shape(M, P, *shape))

Interval n's polynomial in the local variable x = (t - mesh[n]) / (mesh[n+1] - mesh[n]) in [0, 1], as monomial coefficients, lowest degree first.

nodes (ndarray, shape(p))

The nominal node positions in [0, 1], sorted.

coll_setting tuple or None

(divs, choices) for sampled inputs, None for callable inputs.

equation {'vie1', 'vie2', 'vide'} regime {'sampled', 'functional'} continuous bool

Whether the solution space is continuous across breakpoints (VIDE, and VIE-1 with continuous=True).

Here ``shape`` is ``()`` for scalar problems, ``(d,)`` for vector problems and ``(d, m)`` for m right-hand sides. The dtype is complex for complex problems. See Also
  • solve_vie1, solve_vie2, solve_vide: the solvers that return it.
  • to_ppoly: derivatives, integrals and roots.

Examples:

\(g(t) = \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)} y(s)\,ds\) with \(g = \sin t\) has the solution \(y = \cos t + \sin t\). Solve it on four intervals:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import voles
>>> sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u), g=np.sin,
...                        mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
>>> sol.mesh
array([0.  , 0.25, 0.5 , 0.75, 1.  ])
>>> sol.coefficients.shape, sol.node_times.shape
((4, 3), (4, 3))

Evaluate anywhere in \([0, T]\); outside it the result is NaN:

>>> print(f"{sol(0.3):.5f}  {np.cos(0.3) + np.sin(0.3):.5f}")
1.25088  1.25086
>>> sol(1.5)
nan

This (discontinuous) solution has two one-sided limits at each interior breakpoint; sol(t) gives their mean unless asked otherwise:

>>> for side in ("left", "mean", "right"):
...     print(side, f"{sol(0.5, at_breakpoints=side):.5f}")
left 1.35708
mean 1.35703
right 1.35697

Integrals and derivatives through scipy.interpolate.PPoly:

>>> print(f"{sol.to_ppoly().integrate(0, 1):.6f}  {np.sin(1) - np.cos(1) + 1:.6f}")
1.301168  1.301169

class VolterraSolution:
    r"""The solution of a Volterra equation, as returned by the solvers.

    A piecewise polynomial on ``mesh`` (continuous or discontinuous at the
    breakpoints), together with its values on the grid the problem was posed
    on, the collocation data, and a record of the method. Call it to evaluate
    the solution anywhere in ``[0, T]``.

    Users don't construct it; every solver returns one.

    Attributes
    ----------
    t : ndarray, shape (K,)
        The grid the problem was posed on: the sample times ``n * dt`` for
        sampled inputs, the mesh breakpoints for callable inputs. Read-only.
    y : ndarray, shape (K, *shape)
        The solution at ``t``. At an interior breakpoint of a discontinuous
        solution this is the mean of the two one-sided limits, the same
        value ``sol(t)`` gives. Writable; changing it doesn't change the
        solution.
    mesh : ndarray, shape (M + 1,)
        The breakpoints ``0 = t_0 < ... < t_M = T``.
    node_times : ndarray, shape (M, p)
        The collocation times actually used. For sampled inputs the final
        interval may be longer than the others, and its nodes sit on its
        own sample grid, so they can differ from ``mesh[n] + nodes * h_n``.
    node_values : ndarray, shape (M, p, *shape)
        The solution at ``node_times``: the collocation values.
    coefficients : ndarray, shape (M, P, *shape)
        Interval n's polynomial in the local variable
        ``x = (t - mesh[n]) / (mesh[n+1] - mesh[n])`` in ``[0, 1]``, as
        monomial coefficients, lowest degree first.
    nodes : ndarray, shape (p,)
        The nominal node positions in ``[0, 1]``, sorted.
    coll_setting : tuple or None
        ``(divs, choices)`` for sampled inputs, ``None`` for callable inputs.
    equation : {"vie1", "vie2", "vide"}
    regime : {"sampled", "functional"}
    continuous : bool
        Whether the solution space is continuous across breakpoints (VIDE,
        and VIE-1 with ``continuous=True``).

    Here ``shape`` is ``()`` for scalar problems, ``(d,)`` for vector
    problems and ``(d, m)`` for m right-hand sides. The dtype is complex for
    complex problems.

    See Also
    --------
    - [solve_vie1][voles.solve_vie1], [solve_vie2][voles.solve_vie2],
      [solve_vide][voles.solve_vide]: the solvers that return it.
    - [to_ppoly][voles.VolterraSolution.to_ppoly]: derivatives, integrals and roots.

    Examples
    --------
    $g(t) = \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)} y(s)\,ds$ with $g = \sin t$ has the solution
    $y = \cos t + \sin t$. Solve it on four intervals:

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> import voles
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u), g=np.sin,
    ...                        mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
    >>> sol.mesh
    array([0.  , 0.25, 0.5 , 0.75, 1.  ])
    >>> sol.coefficients.shape, sol.node_times.shape
    ((4, 3), (4, 3))

    Evaluate anywhere in $[0, T]$; outside it the result is NaN:

    >>> print(f"{sol(0.3):.5f}  {np.cos(0.3) + np.sin(0.3):.5f}")
    1.25088  1.25086
    >>> sol(1.5)
    nan

    This (discontinuous) solution has two one-sided limits at each interior
    breakpoint; ``sol(t)`` gives their mean unless asked otherwise:

    >>> for side in ("left", "mean", "right"):
    ...     print(side, f"{sol(0.5, at_breakpoints=side):.5f}")
    left 1.35708
    mean 1.35703
    right 1.35697

    Integrals and derivatives through `scipy.interpolate.PPoly`:

    >>> print(f"{sol.to_ppoly().integrate(0, 1):.6f}  {np.sin(1) - np.cos(1) + 1:.6f}")
    1.301168  1.301169
    """

    equation: Literal["vie1", "vie2", "vide"]
    regime: Literal["sampled", "functional"]
    continuous: bool
    coll_setting: Optional[Tuple[int, List[int]]]
    # State set by `_build` (and restored by unpickling).
    _coef: np.ndarray
    _mesh: np.ndarray
    _nodes: np.ndarray
    _local_nodes: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_times: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_values: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_layout: Optional[tuple]
    _y: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _t: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _dt: Optional[float]
    _n: Optional[int]
    _d: int
    _m: int

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        raise TypeError("VolterraSolution objects are returned by the solvers; "
                        "they are not constructed directly")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ building

    @classmethod
    def _build(cls, *, coefficients, mesh, nodes, equation, regime, continuous, d, m,
               local_nodes=None, node_times=None, node_layout=None, coll_setting=None,
               y=None, node_values=None, dt=None, n_samples=None, copy_mesh=True):
        """The solvers' constructor.

        ``local_nodes`` (M, p): each interval's node positions in its local
        variable, which `node_values` evaluates at when the solver hasn't
        supplied them; ``node_times`` (M, p) the times. Instead of both, the
        sampled builder passes ``node_layout`` (a tuple for `_sampled_layout`),
        and they are computed on first access. Sampled regime: ``y`` (the
        values on the sample grid), ``dt`` and ``n_samples`` are required.
        Functional regime: ``y`` is computed on first access, at the
        breakpoints. ``copy_mesh=False`` is for a mesh voles built itself."""
        if equation not in _EQUATIONS or regime not in _REGIMES:
            raise ValueError(f"bad equation/regime {equation!r}/{regime!r}")
        self = cls.__new__(cls)
        coef = np.asarray(coefficients)
        if not np.issubdtype(coef.dtype, np.complexfloating):
            coef = coef.astype(float, copy=False)
        self._coef = _read_only(coef, copy=False)          # computed by the engine
        self._mesh = _read_only(mesh, dtype=float, copy=copy_mesh)   # may alias user data
        M = len(self._mesh) - 1
        if self._coef.shape[0] != M or M < 1:
            raise ValueError(f"{self._coef.shape[0]} coefficient blocks for {M} mesh intervals")
        self._node_layout = node_layout
        if node_layout is None:
            self._set_node_arrays(local_nodes, node_times)
        else:
            self._local_nodes = self._node_times = None
        self._nodes = _read_only(np.sort(np.asarray(nodes, dtype=float)))
        self._node_values = (None if node_values is None
                             else _read_only(node_values, copy=False))   # engine output
        self.equation = equation
        self.regime = regime
        self.continuous = bool(continuous)
        self.coll_setting = (None if coll_setting is None
                             else (int(coll_setting[0]), [int(c) for c in coll_setting[1]]))
        self._d, self._m = int(d), int(m)
        if regime == "sampled":
            if y is None or dt is None or n_samples is None:
                raise ValueError("the sampled regime needs y, dt and n_samples")
            self._y = np.asarray(y)
            self._dt, self._n = float(dt), int(n_samples)
        else:
            self._y = None if y is None else np.asarray(y)
            self._dt = self._n = None
        self._t = None
        return self

    def __getstate__(self):
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        state["_t"] = None               # rebuilt on demand
        return state

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ attributes

    @property
    def mesh(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._mesh

    @property
    def coefficients(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._coef

    def _set_node_arrays(self, local_nodes, node_times):
        self._local_nodes = _read_only(local_nodes, dtype=float, copy=False)
        self._node_times = _read_only(node_times, dtype=float, copy=False)
        if (self._local_nodes.shape != self._node_times.shape
                or self._node_times.shape[0] != len(self._mesh) - 1):
            raise ValueError("node arrays must have shape (M, p)")

    def _nodes_local_and_times(self) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        if self._local_nodes is None or self._node_times is None:
            assert self._node_layout is not None
            self._set_node_arrays(*_sampled_layout(*self._node_layout))
        assert self._local_nodes is not None and self._node_times is not None
        return self._local_nodes, self._node_times

    @property
    def node_times(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._nodes_local_and_times()[1]

    @property
    def nodes(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._nodes

    @property
    def t(self) -> np.ndarray:
        t = self._t
        if t is None:
            if self.regime == "sampled":
                assert self._n is not None and self._dt is not None
                t = _read_only(np.arange(self._n) * self._dt)
            else:
                t = self._mesh
            self._t = t
        return t

    @property
    def y(self) -> np.ndarray:
        y = self._y
        if y is None:                             # functional regime, first access
            y = np.asarray(self(self._mesh))
            self._y = y
        return y

    @property
    def node_values(self) -> np.ndarray:
        nv = self._node_values
        if nv is None:
            x = self._nodes_local_and_times()[0]                # (M, p)
            c = self._coef                                      # (M, P, *cs)
            extra = (1,) * (c.ndim - 2)
            xb = x.reshape(x.shape + extra)
            out = np.broadcast_to(c[:, -1][:, None], x.shape + c.shape[2:])
            for k in range(c.shape[1] - 2, -1, -1):
                out = out * xb + c[:, k][:, None]
            nv = self._node_values = _read_only(out)
        return nv

    @property
    def _shape(self):
        return self._coef.shape[2:]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ evaluation

    def _horner(self, idx, x):
        """Interval ``idx[i]``'s polynomial at local ``x[i]``, without
        gathering an (n, P, *shape) copy of the coefficients."""
        c = self._coef
        xb = x.reshape(x.shape + (1,) * (c.ndim - 2))
        out = c[idx, -1]                  # a fresh gather, so updating in place is safe
        for k in range(c.shape[1] - 2, -1, -1):
            out *= xb                     # same operations as out = out * x + c_k
            out += c[idx, k]
        return out

    def __call__(self, t: ArrayLike, *,
                 at_breakpoints: Literal["mean", "left", "right"] = "mean"
                 ) -> Union[float, complex, np.ndarray]:
        """Evaluate the solution at ``t`` (scalar or array).

        Parameters
        ----------
        t : float or array_like
            Times in ``[0, T]``. Points outside (beyond a rounding-level
            tolerance) give NaN; the solution is never extrapolated.
        at_breakpoints : {"mean", "left", "right"}, optional
            The value at an interior breakpoint, where a discontinuous
            solution has two one-sided limits: their mean (default), the
            limit from the left, or from the right. A point within a few
            ulps of a breakpoint counts as that breakpoint. For a continuous
            solution the three agree to rounding.

        Returns
        -------
        float, complex or ndarray
            A scalar ``t`` gives a Python float or complex for scalar problems
            and an array of shape ``shape`` otherwise; an array ``t`` gives an
            array of shape ``t.shape + shape``.
        """
        mode = _v.choice("at_breakpoints", at_breakpoints, _AT_BREAKPOINTS)
        scalar_input = np.ndim(t) == 0
        t_arr = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
        tf = t_arr.ravel()
        bps = self._mesh
        M = len(bps) - 1
        idx = np.clip(np.searchsorted(bps, tf, side="right") - 1, 0, M - 1)
        x = (tf - bps[idx]) / (bps[idx + 1] - bps[idx])
        out = self._horner(idx, x)
        if M > 1 and tf.size:
            interior = bps[1:-1]
            tol = 4.0 * np.spacing(np.abs(interior))
            j = np.searchsorted(interior, tf)
            lo, hi = np.clip(j - 1, 0, M - 2), np.clip(j, 0, M - 2)
            hit_hi = np.abs(tf - interior[hi]) <= tol[hi]
            hit_lo = np.abs(tf - interior[lo]) <= tol[lo]
            at = hit_hi | hit_lo
            if at.any():
                k = np.where(hit_hi, hi, lo)[at] + 1          # interval to the right
                n = k.size
                left = self._horner(k - 1, np.ones(n))
                right = self._horner(k, np.zeros(n))
                out = np.array(out, copy=True)
                out[at] = (0.5 * (left + right) if mode == "mean"
                           else left if mode == "left" else right)
        # Defined on [t_0, t_M] only. The tolerance is relative to the solved
        # interval, but never below a few ulps of the endpoints, so an exactly
        # computed T passes.
        tol_end = max(1e-12 * float(bps[-1] - bps[0]),
                      4.0 * float(np.spacing(np.max(np.abs(bps)))))
        outside = (tf < bps[0] - tol_end) | (tf > bps[-1] + tol_end)
        if outside.any():
            out = np.array(out, copy=True)
            out[outside] = np.nan
        if scalar_input:
            v = out[0]
            return v.item() if not self._shape else v
        return out.reshape(t_arr.shape + self._shape)

    def to_ppoly(self) -> PPoly:
        """The solution as a `scipy.interpolate.PPoly`.

        Useful for derivatives (``.derivative()``), antiderivatives and
        integrals (``.antiderivative()``, ``.integrate(a, b)``) and roots.
        The trailing axes are the problem's ``shape``. PPoly is
        right-continuous at breakpoints (it uses the right-hand interval's
        polynomial there), and returns NaN outside ``[0, T]``.
        """
        from scipy.interpolate import PPoly
        c = self._coef
        h = np.diff(self._mesh)
        P = c.shape[1]
        scale = h[:, None] ** -np.arange(P)[None, :]             # (M, P): 1 / h^k
        scaled = c * scale.reshape(scale.shape + (1,) * (c.ndim - 2))
        pc = np.ascontiguousarray(np.moveaxis(scaled, 1, 0)[::-1])   # (P, M, *shape)
        return PPoly(pc, self._mesh, extrapolate=False)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        M = len(self._mesh) - 1
        nodes = (f"coll_setting={self.coll_setting}" if self.coll_setting is not None
                 else "coll_nodes=[" + ", ".join(f"{c:.4g}" for c in self._nodes) + "]")
        shape = f", shape={self._shape}" if self._shape else ""
        return (f"<VolterraSolution {self.equation}, {self.regime}, {M} intervals on "
                f"[0, {self._mesh[-1]:.6g}], degree {self._coef.shape[1] - 1}, {nodes}"
                f"{shape}, {self._coef.dtype}>")

solve_vide(*, kernel, a=None, g=None, y0, dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature='product', samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, mesh=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True)

Solve a Volterra integro-differential equation.

\[y'(t) = a(t)\, y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\, y(s)\, ds, \qquad y(0) = y_0\]

by collocation: on each mesh interval \(y\) is a polynomial whose derivative satisfies the equation at the collocation nodes, continuous across the breakpoints.

The inputs are either arrays of samples at \(t = 0, dt, 2\,dt, \ldots\) (the sampled regime) or callables (the functional regime, solved on the breakpoints mesh); see Notes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kernel array_like or callable

\(K\). Sampled: shape (N,), or (N, d, d) for a system of \(d\) equations, at \(u = 0, dt, \ldots, (N-1)\,dt\). Callable: kernel(u) returning a scalar or a (d, d) matrix; it may be vectorised over a 1-D u, which is faster.

required a array_like or callable

\(a\). Sampled: (N,) or (N, d, d). Callable: a(t) returning a scalar or a (d, d) matrix. Default zero.

None g array_like or callable

\(g\). Sampled: (N,), (N, d) or (N, d, m) for \(m\) right-hand sides. Callable: g(t) returning a scalar, (d,) or (d, m). Default zero.

None y0 array_like

\(y(0)\): scalar, (d,), or (d, m) for \(m\) initial values. A (d,) value is shared by all columns of a matrix g, and a (N, d) or (d,)-valued g by all columns of a (d, m) y0.

required dt float

Sampled inputs: the sample spacing. Default 1.0.

1.0 coll_setting int or (int, sequence of int)

Sampled inputs: the collocation nodes choices / divs as (divs, choices), with choices in 0..divs, or a bare divs meaning every point 0..divs. divs also sets the mesh width (see samples_per_interval). Default (2, [0, 1, 2]).

None quadrature ('product', 'collocation')

Sampled inputs: how the integrals are evaluated from the samples. "product" (default) integrates a piecewise polynomial interpolant of the kernel exactly and accepts any mesh width and node set. "collocation" applies the interpolatory rule on the nodes; it is faster but fixes the mesh at divs**2 samples and runs only compiled settings (or the numba fallback).

"product" samples_per_interval int

Sampled inputs: samples per mesh interval. A multiple of divs with product quadrature (default divs); must be divs**2 with collocation quadrature.

None kernel_interp_degree int

Sampled inputs, product quadrature: the degree of the kernel interpolant. Default: the number of nodes.

None mesh array_like

Callable inputs: the mesh breakpoints, strictly increasing from 0 to \(T\). Required for callable inputs.

None coll_nodes array_like

Callable inputs: node positions in \([0, 1]\), e.g. voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(3). Default [0, 1/2, 1].

None kernel_singularity (float, list, dict or callable)

Callable inputs: where the kernel is weakly singular, in \(u = t - s\): a location, a list of locations, {location: alpha} for \(K \sim |u - u_0|^{-\alpha}\) (enables Gauss–Jacobi rules), or a callable returning the singular \(s\)-locations for a time \(t\).

None reuse_adaptive_blocks bool

Callable inputs: on a uniform mesh, reuse adaptive-quadrature blocks across mesh intervals. Default True.

True

Returns:

Type Description VolterraSolution

The solution: sol.t and sol.y on the input grid (the samples, or the mesh breakpoints), sol(t) anywhere in \([0, T]\), plus the collocation data and coefficients.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

An argument of the wrong type (a float where an integer is needed, a non-bool flag, a non-numeric array), or y0 missing.

ValueError

A wrong value: shapes that don't fit, an option from the other regime, an invalid node set, NaN or inf in the data, too few samples for one mesh interval.

NotImplementedError

Mixed callable and sampled inputs, or an uncompiled setting under quadrature="collocation" with no fallback.

LinAlgError

A collocation system is singular.

Warns:

Type Description AccuracyWarning

A singularity declared on a uniform mesh.

PerformanceWarning

The numba fallback is used.

VolesWarning

A kernel_singularity location outside \([0, T]\).

See Also
  • solve_vie1, solve_vie2: the other two equations.
  • VolterraSolution: the returned object.
  • optimal_graded_mesh: a mesh for a weakly singular kernel.
  • gauss_legendre_nodes: node sets for coll_nodes.
Notes

The regime is chosen by the input types: arrays give the sampled regime (dt, coll_setting, quadrature, samples_per_interval, kernel_interp_degree apply), callables the functional regime (mesh, coll_nodes, kernel_singularity, reuse_adaptive_blocks apply). An option from the other regime is an error. Mixing callable and sampled inputs is not supported yet.

Examples:

Sampled data: \(y' = \int_0^t y(s)\,ds\) with \(y(0) = 1\) is \(y'' = y\), \(y'(0) = 0\), so \(y = \cosh t\).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import voles
>>> t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
>>> sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.ones_like(t), y0=1.0, dt=t[1])
>>> print(f"{sol(1.0):.8f}  {np.cosh(1.0):.8f}")
1.54308063  1.54308063

Callables: \(y' = -\int_0^t y(s)\,ds\) with \(y(0) = 1\) gives \(y = \cos t\). The solution is continuous, and its derivative comes from VolterraSolution.to_ppoly:

>>> sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=lambda u: -np.ones_like(u), y0=1.0,
...                        mesh=np.linspace(0, np.pi, 21))
>>> sol.continuous
True
>>> print(f"{sol(np.pi / 3):.4f}  {sol.to_ppoly().derivative()(np.pi / 3):.4f}")
0.5000  -0.8660

def solve_vide(*, kernel: Data, a: Optional[Data] = None, g: Optional[Data] = None,
               y0: ArrayLike,
               dt: float = 1.0, coll_setting: CollSetting = None,
               quadrature: Quadrature = "product",
               samples_per_interval: Optional[int] = None,
               kernel_interp_degree: Optional[int] = None,
               mesh: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, coll_nodes: Optional[ArrayLike] = None,
               kernel_singularity: KernelSingularity = None,
               reuse_adaptive_blocks: bool = True) -> VolterraSolution:
    r"""Solve a Volterra integro-differential equation.

    $$y'(t) = a(t)\, y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\, y(s)\, ds, \qquad y(0) = y_0$$

    by collocation: on each mesh interval $y$ is a polynomial whose
    derivative satisfies the equation at the collocation nodes, continuous
    across the breakpoints.

    The inputs are either arrays of samples at $t = 0, dt, 2\,dt, \ldots$
    (the *sampled* regime) or callables (the *functional* regime, solved on
    the breakpoints ``mesh``); see Notes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    kernel : array_like or callable
        $K$. Sampled: shape ``(N,)``, or ``(N, d, d)`` for a system of $d$
        equations, at $u = 0, dt, \ldots, (N-1)\,dt$. Callable: ``kernel(u)``
        returning a scalar or a ``(d, d)`` matrix; it may be vectorised
        over a 1-D ``u``, which is faster.
    a : array_like or callable, optional
        $a$. Sampled: ``(N,)`` or ``(N, d, d)``. Callable: ``a(t)`` returning
        a scalar or a ``(d, d)`` matrix. Default zero.
    g : array_like or callable, optional
        $g$. Sampled: ``(N,)``, ``(N, d)`` or ``(N, d, m)`` for $m$
        right-hand sides. Callable: ``g(t)`` returning a scalar, ``(d,)`` or
        ``(d, m)``. Default zero.
    y0 : array_like
        $y(0)$: scalar, ``(d,)``, or ``(d, m)`` for $m$ initial values. A
        ``(d,)`` value is shared by all columns of a matrix ``g``, and a
        ``(N, d)`` or ``(d,)``-valued ``g`` by all columns of a ``(d, m)``
        ``y0``.
    dt : float, optional

    PerformanceWarning

    VolesWarning

    (``dt``, ``coll_setting``, ``quadrature``, ``samples_per_interval``,
    ``kernel_interp_degree`` apply), callables the functional regime

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> import voles
    >>> t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.ones_like(t), y0=1.0, dt=t[1])
