docs.title: 1.6 Exceptions raised, by type
docs.text: Type Count of sites Used for ValueError 141 nearly everything: shapes, ranges, non-integers, mutually exclusive args, unknown quadrature, non-convergent node sets, wrong-type arguments such as coll_divs=2.0 or show_warnings of the wrong type (not checked at all) TypeError 9 non-callable kernel/g/a; internal _SolutionFunction construction; Python's own for missing required kwargs NotImplementedError 6 collocation setting not compiled and no fallback ImportError 6 D extension not found; scipy missing numpy.linalg.LinAlgError 2 singular collocation system RuntimeError 1 nonzero return code from the D extension (_dlang.py:246) — undocumented

docs.title: 1.7 Warnings emitted, by channel
docs.text:
Channel Count Conditions print("warning: ...") to stdout 15 sites Numba fallback; soln_init_value ignored; ρ = 1 reduced order; g(0) ≠ 0; K(0) small (VIE-1 collocation quadrature); singularity declared on a uniform mesh; singularity outside [0, T]; stale D extension lacking the lag-block driver warnings.warn(DeprecationWarning) 1 site return_polys scipy IntegrationWarning pass-through from adaptive quadrature in the callable family (partly suppressed under reuse_adaptive_blocks) numpy ComplexWarning escalated to ValueError callable family, when sampling missed a complex return

show_warnings gates only the print channel. None of the printed warnings has a category, can be filtered, turned into an error, or captured by pytest.warns.

docs.title: Part 2 — Findings
docs.text: Severity: A = would block a 1.0 at NumPy/SciPy review standard; B = should fix before 1.0, breaking changes need a deprecation cycle; C = polish, can follow 1.0.

docs.title: Lens 1: Error and warning model
docs.text:
F1 (A). Warnings are print() statements. Fifteen diagnostic sites write "warning: ..." to stdout. They cannot be filtered, promoted to errors, captured in tests, or silenced per category; show_warnings=False is the only control and it is all-or-nothing. In a Jupyter cell or a batch job the message is invisible or lost. Proposed: define VolesWarning(UserWarning) with two or three subclasses (e.g. ConvergenceWarning for ρ = 1, g(0) ≠ 0, K(0) small; PerformanceWarning for the Numba fallback and the stale-extension notice; MeshWarning for the uniform-mesh hint) and emit through warnings.warn(..., stacklevel=2). Then deprecate show_warnings (see F2).

F2 (B). show_warnings duplicates the standard warnings machinery. Once F1 is done, show_warnings=False is warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=VolesWarning). Keep the parameter through 1.0 as a convenience if you like, but define it as exactly that filter so the two can never disagree. SciPy has no such flag on any solver.

F3 (B). ValueError is used where TypeError belongs. coll_divs=2.0, coll_choices=[0.5], order=1.5, p=2.0 all raise ValueError for what is a type problem. Python convention and NumPy/SciPy practice: wrong type → TypeError, right type wrong value → ValueError. Conversely time_step="0.1" escapes validation and raises TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'float' from the comparison. show_warnings="no" and return_function=1 are accepted without comment. Decide the rule once (a one-line policy in the contract doc) and apply it in a single _validate helper per parameter.

F4 (B). RuntimeError from the D extension is undocumented. _dlang.py:246 raises RuntimeError(f"{func_name} returned error code {ret}"). No docstring lists it, and the message is not actionable for a user. Either map the known codes to the documented exceptions or document it.

F5 (B). soln_init_value=None on solve_VIDE silently produces an all-NaN solution. _scalar_init(None) goes through np.asarray(None, dtype=float) → nan. The parameter is documented as required and is required syntactically, but an explicit None (easy to produce from a config dict) is accepted. Should raise.

F6 (C). NaN and inf in the data propagate silently. kernel_values or g_values containing NaN/inf yield an all-NaN result with no diagnostic. The tests codify "raises or propagates". SciPy's solve_ivp and quad do not check either, so this is defensible, but the Raises section should say so explicitly ("non-finite input is not checked"), or a cheap np.isfinite check should raise ValueError.

docs.title: Lens 2: Consistency across the six solvers
docs.text:
F7 (A). The two families name the same concept differently.

Concept array family callable family kernel kernel_values kernel forcing g_values g coefficient a_values a time grid time_step (+ implicit N) mesh_breakpoints initial value soln_init_value soln_init_value node set coll_divs, coll_choices coll_divs, coll_choices, coll_nodes

The _values suffix is justified for the array family only because the same names mean callables elsewhere. A single family with kernel= accepting either an array or a callable (dispatch on callable(kernel)) would remove the prefix function_ and the suffix _values together. See F9 before deciding.

F8 (A). coll_divs means two different things in the two families. Array family: a mesh interval is coll_divs**2 samples (collocation quadrature) or mesh_samples samples, with coll_divs sub-intervals. Callable family: coll_divs only sets node positions k/coll_divs; the mesh is mesh_breakpoints. The docs flag this in a "Convention note" because it bites. For 1.0 the node set should be expressed one way everywhere. The callable family's coll_nodes (floats in [0,1]) is the general form; coll_divs/coll_choices is a rational special case of it. Proposed: a single nodes= parameter accepting an array of floats in [0,1] or a string preset ("radau", "gauss", "lobatto", "uniform") with a count, and coll_divs/coll_choices kept only as the array family's sampling parameter under a name that says so (e.g. samples_per_interval).

F9 (A). The two families return different things for "the solution". Array family: values at the input sample times, shape (N, ...). Callable family: values at the collocation nodes, shape (M, p, ...), and no time array. A user of function_solve_* must reconstruct t[n, i] = mesh[n] + c_i * h_n themselves; the docs example does exactly this in a double loop. This is the strongest argument for a result object (F10): res.t and res.y make both families return the same thing, and res.sol is the dense output.

F10 (A). The solution object is a private class with no public name and no repr. type(solution) is voles._solution._SolutionFunction; repr is the default. Users cannot annotate it, isinstance it, or document it. Proposed: a public VolterraResult (or VolterraSolution) modelled on scipy.integrate.OdeResult: attributes t, y, sol (the callable), mesh, nodes, method-style metadata, success/message if you ever add adaptive failure modes, and a useful __repr__. Then return_function is unnecessary: the callable is always available (coefficient storage is already cheap; the Polynomial list is lazy).

F11 (B). Matrix mode is selected by different inputs in different solvers. VIE-1/VIE-2: 3-D g_values. VIDE: 2-D soln_init_value (3-D g_values alone does not select it). Callable VIE-1/2: 2-D return from g. This is documented but asymmetric. With a result object and explicit shapes it is better to select on one rule: trailing axis of g (or y0 where g is absent).

F12 (B). VIE-1's soln_init_value is a conditional parameter with a printed warning when ignored. It only means anything with force_continuous=True. Two parameters that are only valid together is a smell; consider continuous=y0 (None = discontinuous method, a value = continuous method with that initial value), which removes the warning and the "required when" clause.

docs.title: Lens 3: Naming
docs.text:
F13 (B). soln_init_value → y0. Every ODE/IE interface in SciPy, Julia, and MATLAB calls this y0. The equations in the docstrings already write y(0) = y_0.

F14 (B). function_solve_* prefix. Reads as "the function that solves" rather than "solve from functions". If the families stay separate, solve_VIE_2_callable or a callable/sampled keyword is clearer; if merged (F7), the prefix disappears.

F15 (C). VIE_1 / VIE_2 / VIDE casing. Mixed case in function names is non-PEP8 and unusual in NumPy/SciPy (solve_ivp, solve_bvp). solve_vie1, solve_vie2, solve_vide would be conventional. This is a judgement call; the current names are at least internally consistent and searchable. Decide and record it.

F16 (B). fast_coll_settings_* expose a build detail as API. The lists answer "which settings run compiled under quadrature="collocation"", a question that disappeared from the default path in 0.10. They also have an awkward type (list of (int, list)). Either drop them from __all__ (keep as voles.compiled_settings() returning a frozenset, undocumented in the main nav) or deprecate them outright.

F17 (C). _smooth_gl_order in the public signature. A leading-underscore parameter appears in help(), the rendered API pages, and inspect.signature. Move it to a module-level knob or **_internal.

F18 (C). optimal_graded_mesh parameter names. alpha, T, M, order are fine for the audience but inconsistent with the solvers' verbosity (mesh_breakpoints, soln_init_value). n_intervals for M would match. Low priority.

docs.title: Lens 4: Return types and dtype/shape contract
docs.text:
F19 (B). No single written statement of the shape contract. Shapes are scattered across six docstrings. Needed once, in the user guide: time axis first; scalar (), vector (d,), matrix (d, m); kernel (d, d); complex handled by block embedding; float32 upcast; no broadcasting of g against columns except the documented shared-(N, d) case for VIDE. The review found one undocumented asymmetry: VIDE accepts a shared (N, d) forcing for all columns, VIE-1/2 do not.

F20 (C). Scalar solution(t) returns a Python float, array t returns ndarray. Matches np.polynomial.Polynomial behaviour, so acceptable, but say so.

F21 (C). Dense output outside [0, T] is NaN rather than an error. Reasonable and documented. SciPy's OdeSolution extrapolates silently, which is worse. Keep.

docs.title: Lens 5: Defaults and inference
docs.text:
F22 (B). Three different defaults for "what happens when I give only one of coll_divs/coll_choices". The rules (coll_divs alone → all points; coll_choices alone → max entry; neither → (3,[1,2,3]) or (2,[0,1,2])) are sensible and now documented, but they are a consequence of the two-integer encoding. Under F8 they vanish.

F23 (B). Default mesh_samples differs between VIE-1 (coll_divs**2) and VIE-2/VIDE (coll_divs). Justified in the Notes (first-kind amplification), but a researcher comparing a first- and second-kind solve on the same data gets different mesh widths without asking. Fine to keep; needs one sentence in the user guide and a worked example of the trade-off.

F24 (C). quadrature is case-sensitive and the error lists the options. Fine. Consider accepting str.lower().

docs.title: Lens 6: Extensibility
docs.text:
F25 (B). Non-convolution kernels are the announced next feature and the current signatures leave no slot for them. kernel(u) and kernel_values[(N,)] both assume K(t - s). The callable kernel_singularity form already anticipates K(t, s). If 1.0 ships before that feature, the contract doc should reserve the extension (e.g. kernel of two arguments detected by arity, or a convolution: bool flag) so it is not a breaking change later.

F26 (C). quadrature= and coll_nodes= are good extension points. Keyword-only everywhere is good. No positional parameters exist except p in the node helpers, which is fine.

docs.title: Lens 7: Documentation contract
docs.text:
F27 (B). Docstrings have no Examples section and nothing is doctested. optimal_graded_mesh has a non-runnable example with .... SciPy requires a runnable example on every public function and runs them in CI. The pytest-markdown-docs dev dependency suggests the docs pages are tested; the docstrings are not.

F28 (B). Cross-references use double backticks rather than numpydoc's single-backtick role. See ``function_solve_VIE_2``` renders as literal text, not a link, under mkdocstrings. Use ``function_solve_VIE_2`` and addSee Also` sections.

F29 (C). Raises sections list ValueError once with a paragraph of causes. Acceptable, but once F3 lands, split TypeError from ValueError and list RuntimeError (F4) and VolesWarning subclasses under a Warns section.

F30 (C). Type hints are partial and py.typed is absent. The array family has none; the callable family has int = None. For 1.0 either annotate everything and ship py.typed, or strip the partial hints so they do not mislead.

docs.title: Lens 8: Packaging and stability
docs.text:
F31 (A). No written stability or deprecation policy. Nothing in README, CHANGELOG, or CONTRIBUTING says what 1.0 promises. One paragraph: semver on the public names in __all__; numerical results may change in a minor release only when the change is a documented accuracy improvement; deprecations warn for at least one minor release.

F32 (B). No signature-snapshot test. A test that pins inspect.signature of every public callable, and the set of names in __all__, catches accidental breaks from then on.

F33 (C). __version__ comes from installed metadata. Correct for wheels, misleading for editable installs with stale metadata (this checkout reports 0.7.0 from a 0.10.0 source tree). Hatch can write a _version.py at build time; either is fine, just be aware.

F34 (C). [callable] and [numba] extras are redundant with [full]. Already noted as compatibility shims in pyproject.toml. Drop at 1.0.

docs.title: Part 3 — Suggested shape of the 1.0 surface
docs.text:
Not a decision, a strawman to argue with. It resolves F7–F14 and F19 at once.

python notest res = voles.solve_vie2( kernel, # array (N,) / (N,d,d) sampled at t = 0, h, ..., or callable K(u) g=None, # array or callable, same convention as kernel t=None, # float h (uniform sampling) or 1-D mesh breakpoints nodes="radau", # str preset, or array of floats in [0, 1], or (divs, choices) order=3, # number of nodes when `nodes` is a preset singularity=None, # as today's kernel_singularity quadrature="product", mesh_samples=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, ) res.t # times where res.y is reported (sample times, or collocation nodes) res.y # values, shape (len(t), ...) — time axis first, always res.sol # callable dense output, NaN outside [0, T] res.mesh # breakpoints res.nodes # node positions in [0, 1]

solve_vie1 adds continuous=None (a y0 value turns on the continuous method); solve_vide adds a=None and required y0. Everything today's API does is reachable; the six functions become three; return_function, return_polys, show_warnings, soln_init_value, force_continuous, coll_divs, coll_choices, coll_nodes, function_solve_*, and fast_coll_settings_* become deprecation shims for one minor release.

If merging the families is too large a change, the minimum set that still reaches the bar is: F1, F3, F5, F9, F10, F13, F31, F32 — a result object with t/y/sol, real warnings, a type/value error rule, y0, and a policy.

docs.title: Example: Complex-Valued Equations
docs.text:
Pass complex arrays for the kernel, the forcing function and (for the VIDE) the initial value, and the solution is complex. This works for scalar, vector, and matrix problems alike, and for callables that return complex values.

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(41) * dt
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-1j * t), g=np.ones_like(t), dt=dt)
print(sol.y.dtype, type(sol(0.5)))      # complex128 <class 'complex'>

A complex oscillator as a VIDE with callables: \(y' = i\omega y\), \(y(0) = 1\), has the solution \(e^{i\omega t}\).

import numpy as np
import voles

omega = 2.0
sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=lambda u: np.zeros_like(u), a=lambda t: 1j * omega,
                       y0=1.0, mesh=np.linspace(0, 3, 61))
tt = np.linspace(0, 3, 301)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol(tt) - np.exp(1j * omega * tt))):.1e}")

docs.title: Example: Callable inputs and arbitrary meshes
docs.text:
Given callables kernel(u), g(t) and a(t) in place of sampled arrays, the solvers run on any mesh you supply with mesh=, and handle integrable singularities in the kernel.

The breakpoints in mesh are the mesh intervals themselves. The collocation nodes, coll_nodes, are positions in [0, 1] within each interval. For finer resolution, pass more breakpoints.

docs.title: Smooth kernel, arbitrary mesh
docs.text:
The standard VIE-2 example, with callables and a hand-picked non-uniform mesh:

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: np.exp(-u)
g = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))  # exact y(t) = sin(t)

# Non-uniform mesh: more resolution where g is changing fastest
mesh = np.array([0.0, 0.05, 0.12, 0.22, 0.35, 0.50, 0.68, 0.85, 1.0])

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh)

print(sol(0.37), "vs exact", np.sin(0.37))
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
print("max error:", np.max(np.abs(sol(tt) - np.sin(tt))))
print(sol.t is sol.mesh, sol.y.shape)        # the grid is the mesh: (9,)

sol.y holds the solution at the breakpoints, and sol.node_values at the collocation times sol.node_times, shape (M, p).

docs.title: Weakly singular kernel and a graded mesh
docs.text:
For Abel-type kernels \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), declaring the singularity and using optimal_graded_mesh recovers the full collocation convergence order, which a uniform mesh does not achieve.

import numpy as np
import voles

# y(t) = g(t) + int_0^t (t-s)^(-1/2) y(s) ds with exact solution y = sqrt(t)
kernel = lambda u: u**-0.5
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t

nodes = np.array([0, 1, 2]) / 2
mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=30, order=len(nodes))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes,
                       kernel_singularity=0.0)     # declare the singularity at u = 0

err = np.max(np.abs(sol.node_values - np.sqrt(sol.node_times)))
print(f"max error at the collocation times: {err:.2e}")

Declaring the singularity matters. The quadrature nodes are all interior, so an undeclared endpoint singularity usually does not raise an error; the solver quietly loses convergence order, and spends longer in adaptive fallbacks, instead. If the kernel ever evaluates to inf or nan at a quadrature node, a ValueError points you to kernel_singularity, but do not rely on that safety net: declare every integrable singularity you know about. Declaring a singularity on a near-uniform mesh gives a voles.AccuracyWarning suggesting optimal_graded_mesh.

docs.title: Known power law? Declare it for a much faster build
docs.text:
If you also know the singularity's exponent, use the dict form kernel_singularity={location: alpha} for \(K(u) \sim |u - u_0|^{-\alpha}\). Blocks touching the singularity are then integrated by deterministic Gauss–Jacobi rules with the singular factor absorbed into the quadrature weight. On the Abel problem above, with 30 intervals, this makes the solve about 8× faster on the graded mesh (16 ms instead of 132 ms), with the same accuracy. On a uniform mesh the default reuse_adaptive_blocks=True already recovers most of that (16 ms), and the dict form halves it again (8 ms):

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: u**-0.5
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t   # exact y = sqrt(t)
mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=30, order=3)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh,
                       kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})   # K(u) ~ u^(-1/2) near u = 0

A wrongly declared exponent is caught by a two-order acceptance check and falls back to the adaptive treatment automatically, so the dict form is never less accurate than the location-only form. Relatedly, on uniform meshes reuse_adaptive_blocks=True (the default) speeds up the location-only (adaptive) path by reusing adaptive blocks across the Toeplitz assembly, at the price of deviations bounded by the quadrature tolerance (~1e-8); with a fully declared dict form it has no effect.

docs.title: Choosing collocation nodes
docs.text:
coll_nodes takes any distinct positions in [0, 1] ((0, 1] for VIE-1). The classical families come from gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes and lobatto_nodes:

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: np.exp(-u)
g = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))  # exact y(t) = sin(t)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 21),
                       coll_nodes=voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(3))

Gauss–Legendre nodes give mesh-point superconvergence (order 2p) for the VIDE. For VIE-2 the collocation solution is not superconvergent at the mesh points, but with Radau IIA nodes its left limit there is (order 2p − 1, sol(t, at_breakpoints="left")); see Values at breakpoints. For VIE-1 prefer radau_iia_nodes with the default discontinuous method: they have the full order for every p, while Gauss–Legendre nodes lose an order for even p (see VIE-1 admissibility).

docs.title: Vector-valued kernel
docs.text:
A kernel(u) returning a (d, d) matrix and a g(t) returning (d,):

import numpy as np
import voles

d = 2
identity = np.eye(d)
# np.multiply.outer gives a (d, d) matrix for scalar u and an (n, d, d) stack
# for an array of u values; the solver then assembles the weights of a whole
# mesh row in one call. (np.exp(-u) * identity would only accept scalars and
# runs several times slower.)
kernel = lambda u: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), identity)
g_s = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))
g = lambda t: np.array([g_s(t), g_s(t)])

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 21))

print(sol(0.5).shape)                     # (2,)
print(sol(np.linspace(0, 1, 5)).shape)    # (5, 2)

docs.title: Matrix-valued: many right-hand sides at once
docs.text:
To solve several right-hand sides that share the same kernel, return a (d, m) array from g(t) (or, for solve_vide, pass a (d, m) y0). The kernel weight tensor, the expensive part to build, is computed once and reused across all m columns, so this is much cheaper than m separate calls.

import numpy as np
import voles

d = 2
identity = np.eye(d)
kernel = lambda u: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), identity)   # vectorised, see above

# Two right-hand sides (m = 2), stacked column-wise into a (d, m) array.
def g(t):
    g0 = np.array([np.sin(t), np.cos(t)])
    g1 = np.array([t, 1.0 + 0.0 * t])
    return np.column_stack([g0, g1])   # shape (d, m)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 21))

print(sol.node_values.shape)              # (M, p, d, m) == (20, 3, 2, 2)
print(sol(0.5).shape)                     # (d, m) == (2, 2)
print(sol(np.linspace(0, 1, 5)).shape)    # (5, 2, 2)

Matrix problems need a (d, d) matrix kernel. Complex kernels, g, a and initial values work here too.

solve_vie1 and solve_vide take callables the same way. solve_vide also takes an a callable and requires y0; solve_vie1 has the optional continuous=True method, which needs y0: (d, m) in the matrix case, or (d,) to share one initial value across the columns.

docs.title: Example: Vector- and Matrix-Valued Equations
docs.text:
All solvers can solve for vector-valued and matrix-valued functions \(y(t)\). When \(y(t)\) is a \(d\)-dimensional vector, \(g(t)\) is also a \(d\)-dimensional vector and \(K(t)\) and \(a(t)\) are \(d \times d\) matrices. When \(y(t)\) is a \(d \times m\) matrix (\(m\) right-hand sides solved together), \(g(t)\) is a \(d \times m\) matrix and \(K(t)\) and \(a(t)\) are still \(d \times d\).

The case is detected from the shapes: of the arrays for sampled inputs, of the callables' return values otherwise. A problem is matrix-valued when g or y0 has a column axis; an input without one is shared by every column. The kernel's work is shared across the \(m\) columns, so a matrix solve is much cheaper than \(m\) separate calls. Shapes are summarised on the Conventions page.

docs.title: A 2×2 system from samples
docs.text:
A 2×2 VIE-1 with constant kernel \(K = \begin{bmatrix} 3/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 3/2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(g(t) = [t + \tfrac{3}{2}t^2,\ t - \tfrac{1}{2}t^2]\), and exact solution \(y(t) = [1 + 2t,\ 1]\):

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
t = np.arange(91) * dt
N = len(t)

kernel = np.full((N, 2, 2), [[1.5, -0.5], [-0.5, 1.5]])
g = np.column_stack([t + 1.5 * t**2, t - 0.5 * t**2])      # (N, 2)

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=kernel, g=g, dt=dt)
print(sol.y.shape)                                          # (91, 2)
exact = np.column_stack([1 + 2 * t, np.ones(N)])
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - exact)):.2e}")
print(sol(0.55))                                            # an array of shape (2,)

docs.title: Several right-hand sides at once
docs.text:
Three initial values for the same VIDE system, \(y' = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s) y(s)\,ds\), with a shared vector forcing \(g\): y0 of shape (d, m) makes the problem matrix-valued, and the (N, d) forcing is used for every column.

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(201) * dt
N, d = len(t), 2
A = np.array([[-1.0, 0.5], [0.2, -0.8]])
kernel = np.exp(-t)[:, None, None] * A                     # (N, 2, 2)
g = np.column_stack([np.cos(t), np.zeros(N)])              # (N, 2), shared
y0 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0, 2.0],
               [0.0, 1.0, -1.0]])                          # (2, 3): three columns

sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=kernel, g=g, y0=y0, dt=dt)
print(sol.y.shape)                                         # (201, 2, 3)

# Each column is the vector problem with that initial value:
col = voles.solve_vide(kernel=kernel, g=g, y0=y0[:, 2], dt=dt)
print(np.max(np.abs(sol.y[..., 2] - col.y)))

docs.title: Callables
docs.text:
A kernel callable returning a (d, d) matrix, and g(t) returning (d,) or (d, m). Write the kernel so it also accepts a 1-D array of lags, returning the stacked matrices, and the solver uses it vectorised, which is much faster: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A) does this, while np.exp(-u) * A works only for scalar u.

import numpy as np
import voles

A = np.array([[-1.0, 0.5], [0.2, -0.8]])
kernel = lambda u: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A)

def g(t):                                                  # two right-hand sides
    return np.column_stack([[np.sin(t), np.cos(t)], [t, 1.0]])   # (2, 2)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 21))
print(sol.node_values.shape)                               # (20, 3, 2, 2)
print(sol(0.5).shape, sol(np.linspace(0, 1, 5)).shape)     # (2, 2) (5, 2, 2)

docs.title: Example: Working with the Solution
docs.text:
Every solver returns a VolterraSolution: on each mesh interval the solution is an explicit polynomial, fixed by requiring the equation to hold at the collocation nodes. The object evaluates it, exposes its pieces, and converts it to a scipy.interpolate.PPoly for calculus.

import numpy as np
import voles

# y(t) = sin(t) satisfies this VIDE with K(u) = exp(-u), a(t) = -1
dt = 0.1
t = np.arange(89) * dt
g = 1.5 * np.cos(t) + 0.5 * np.sin(t) - 0.5 * np.exp(-t)
sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=-np.ones_like(t), g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)
print(sol)

docs.title: Evaluating
docs.text:
sol(t) takes a scalar or an array, anywhere in \([0, T]\); outside it the result is NaN, never an extrapolation. sol.y holds the values on the input grid sol.t (here the samples).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
t = np.arange(89) * dt
g = 1.5 * np.cos(t) + 0.5 * np.sin(t) - 0.5 * np.exp(-t)
sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=-np.ones_like(t), g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)

print(f"y(0.25) = {sol(0.25):.6f},  exact {np.sin(0.25):.6f}")
print(sol(np.array([0.0, 4.0, 100.0])))          # the last is nan
print(np.max(np.abs(sol(sol.t) - sol.y)))        # the same values, to rounding

docs.title: Derivatives and integrals
docs.text:
sol.to_ppoly() returns the same piecewise polynomial as a scipy.interpolate.PPoly, which differentiates, integrates and finds roots:

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
t = np.arange(89) * dt
g = 1.5 * np.cos(t) + 0.5 * np.sin(t) - 0.5 * np.exp(-t)
sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=-np.ones_like(t), g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)

pp = sol.to_ppoly()
print(f"y'(0.25) = {pp.derivative()(0.25):.6f},  exact {np.cos(0.25):.6f}")
print(f"integral over [0, pi] = {pp.integrate(0, np.pi):.6f},  exact 2")
print("zeros:", pp.roots())                      # 0, π and 2π

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
attribute shape mesh (M + 1,) the breakpoints coefficients (M, P, ...) interval n's polynomial in the local variable x = (t − tₙ)/hₙ ∈ [0, 1], monomial, lowest degree first node_times (M, p) the collocation times node_values (M, p, ...) the solution there nodes (p,) the node positions in [0, 1]

So interval n's polynomial evaluates as np.polynomial.polynomial.polyval(x, sol.coefficients[n]):

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
t = np.arange(89) * dt
g = 1.5 * np.cos(t) + 0.5 * np.sin(t) - 0.5 * np.exp(-t)
sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=-np.ones_like(t), g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)

n, tq = 3, 0.65
x = (tq - sol.mesh[n]) / (sol.mesh[n + 1] - sol.mesh[n])
print(np.polynomial.polynomial.polyval(x, sol.coefficients[n]), sol(tq))
print(sol.node_times[n], sol.node_values[n])

docs.title: Values at breakpoints
docs.text:
VIE-1 and VIE-2 solutions are in general discontinuous at the breakpoints. There sol(t) reports the mean of the two one-sided limits; ask for either limit with at_breakpoints:

import numpy as np
import voles

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u), g=np.sin, mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
for side in ("left", "mean", "right"):
    print(side, sol(0.5, at_breakpoints=side))
print("exact", np.cos(0.5) + np.sin(0.5))

Which convention is the most accurate depends on the node set; see Values at breakpoints. to_ppoly() is right-continuous: at a breakpoint it uses the polynomial of the interval on the right.

docs.title: Example: Product integration for sampled kernels
docs.text:
With sampled inputs the kernel is given as samples K(u) on a grid of spacing dt. With quadrature="collocation" every integral in the collocation equations is evaluated with the interpolatory rule on the collocation nodes themselves (Brunner 2004, Section 2.4.5). That rule needs the kernel at the scaled nodes of each partial interval, which fall on samples only when the mesh is divs**2 samples wide, for coll_setting=(divs, choices), so:

  • the mesh width is divs**2 * dt, and at a fixed sampling rate an order-\(m\) method carries an error constant \(\text{divs}^{m}\) times larger than the same method on a mesh divs samples wide;
  • only every divs-th sample of the data enters the history sums.

quadrature="product" removes the constraint in the classical way (Linz, BIT 11, 1971; de Hoog and Weiss, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 10, 1973): the kernel is replaced by its piecewise-polynomial interpolant of degree kernel_interp_degree on the data grid (default: the number of collocation nodes) and its products with the collocation polynomial are integrated exactly. The mesh can then be any multiple samples_per_interval of divs samples wide, every sample is used, any convergent node set works without the numba fallback, and the FFT-accelerated history of the D extension is still used. Product integration is the default quadrature of all three solvers. The default mesh is the finest one, samples_per_interval=divs, for solve_vie2 and solve_vide; for solve_vie1 it stays at divs**2 samples, because inverting a first-kind equation amplifies errors in the data by roughly the inverse of the mesh width (see below). The collocation quadrature remains available as quadrature="collocation"; it runs in compiled code specialised per setting and is a few times faster.

docs.title: A first-kind equation on coarsely sampled data
docs.text:
The Rubin model (a particle at the end of a semi-infinite harmonic chain) has the correlation function \(C(t) = J_1(2t)/t\) and the memory kernel \(\mathcal{K}(t) = -C(t)\), related by \(\dot C(t) = \int_0^t C(t-s)\mathcal{K}(s)ds\). Sampled at dt = 0.125, about 25 samples per oscillation period, the collocation quadrature puts the order-3 method on a mesh of width 1.125.

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import j1, jv
import voles

dt = 0.125
times = dt * np.arange(32 * 3**2 + 1)
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    C = j1(2 * times) / times                # kernel
    C_dot = -2 * jv(2, 2 * times) / times    # right-hand side
    K_exact = -j1(2 * times) / times
C[0], C_dot[0], K_exact[0] = 1.0, 0.0, -1.0

common = dict(kernel=C, g=C_dot, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))

K_coll = voles.solve_vie1(quadrature="collocation", **common)   # mesh 9 samples wide
K_prod = voles.solve_vie1(samples_per_interval=3, **common)     # product: 3 samples wide

err_coll = np.max(np.abs(K_coll.y - K_exact))
err_prod = np.max(np.abs(K_prod.y - K_exact))
print(f"collocation quadrature: max error {err_coll:.1e}")
print(f"product integration:    max error {err_prod:.1e}")
assert err_prod < err_coll / 10

samples_per_interval chooses the mesh explicitly. With samples_per_interval=9 the mesh is the same as the collocation quadrature's, but the integrals now use all nine samples of each interval rather than three of them:

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import j1, jv
import voles

dt = 0.125
times = dt * np.arange(32 * 9 + 1)
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    C = j1(2 * times) / times
    C_dot = -2 * jv(2, 2 * times) / times
    K_exact = -j1(2 * times) / times
C[0], C_dot[0], K_exact[0] = 1.0, 0.0, -1.0

K_prod9 = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=C, g=C_dot, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]),
                           quadrature="product", samples_per_interval=9)
print(f"product integration, samples_per_interval=9: max error "
      f"{np.max(np.abs(K_prod9.y - K_exact)):.1e}")

Any input length of at least samples_per_interval + 1 is accepted; as for the default quadrature, leftover samples past the last regular mesh interval are absorbed by stretching that interval, so the solution covers every sample.

Noisy data and first-kind equations. Inverting a first-kind equation amplifies errors in the data by roughly the inverse of the mesh width, so on noisy data the finest mesh is not automatically the best choice. samples_per_interval is the knob: larger values trade resolution for a milder amplification; Conventions has measurements. The second-kind equation and the VIDE below are well posed and have no such trade-off.

docs.title: Propagating with a sampled kernel: the VIDE
docs.text:
The same keywords apply to solve_vie2 and solve_vide. Here the memory kernel \(K(u) = -e^{-u/2}\) is sampled and the correlation function is propagated forward from \(y(0) = 1\); the exact solution satisfies \(y'' + y'/2 + y = 0\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
times = dt * np.arange(20 * 3**2 + 1)
kernel = -np.exp(-times / 2)
omega = np.sqrt(1 - 1 / 16)
exact = np.exp(-times / 4) * (np.cos(omega * times) + np.sin(omega * times) / (4 * omega))

common = dict(kernel=kernel, y0=1.0, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))
y_coll = voles.solve_vide(quadrature="collocation", **common)
y_prod = voles.solve_vide(**common)                 # product integration is the default

err_coll = np.max(np.abs(y_coll.y - exact))
err_prod = np.max(np.abs(y_prod.y - exact))
print(f"collocation quadrature: max error {err_coll:.1e}")
print(f"product integration:    max error {err_prod:.1e}")
assert err_prod < err_coll / 5

Because product integration evaluates the weights in Python from the samples and only needs the D extension for the stepping, node sets that are not compiled into the extension are also available:

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.1
times = dt * np.arange(20 * 5 + 1)
kernel = -np.exp(-times / 2)
y5 = voles.solve_vide(kernel=kernel, y0=1.0, dt=dt, coll_setting=(5, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
omega = np.sqrt(1 - 1 / 16)
exact = np.exp(-times / 4) * (np.cos(omega * times) + np.sin(omega * times) / (4 * omega))
assert np.max(np.abs(y5.y - exact)) < 1e-4

docs.title: Example: Volterra Integro-Differential Equation
docs.text:
Solve the VIDE

\[y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\]

with \(a(t) = \frac{1}{1+t^2}\), \(K(u) = e^{-u}\), and \(g(t)\) chosen so the exact solution is \(y(t) = \sin(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(91) * dt                 # 91 samples
a = 1.0 / (1.0 + t**2)
g = (np.cos(t)
     - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))
     - np.sin(t) / (1.0 + t**2))

sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=a, g=g, y0=0.0,      # sin(0) = 0
                       dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))

print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.2e}")
assert np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))) < 1e-3

# The VIDE solution is continuous; evaluate it anywhere in [0, T].
print(f"y(0.5) = {sol(0.5):.6f}  (exact {np.sin(0.5):.6f})")

docs.title: Example: Type-1 Volterra Integral Equation
docs.text:
Solve the VIE-1

\[g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\]

with \(K(u) = e^u\) (as a function of the lag \(u = t - s\)), \(g(t) = \sin(t)\), whose exact solution is \(y(t) = \cos(t) - \sin(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(91) * dt                 # 91 samples

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(t), g=np.sin(t), dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))

exact = np.cos(t) - np.sin(t)
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - exact)):.2e}")
assert np.max(np.abs(sol.y - exact)) < 1e-3

# The solution is a piecewise polynomial: evaluate it anywhere in [0, T].
print(f"y(0.5) = {sol(0.5):.6f}  (exact {np.cos(0.5) - np.sin(0.5):.6f})")

The same equation with callables, on a mesh of 30 intervals and the Radau IIA nodes, which give the first-kind method its full order (see Conventions):

import numpy as np
import voles

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp, g=np.sin, mesh=np.linspace(0, 0.9, 31),
                       coll_nodes=voles.radau_iia_nodes(3))
tt = np.linspace(0, 0.9, 200)
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol(tt) - (np.cos(tt) - np.sin(tt)))):.2e}")

docs.title: Example: Type-2 Volterra Integral Equation
docs.text:
Solve the VIE-2

\[y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\]

with \(K(u) = e^{-u}\) (as a function of the lag \(u = t - s\)) and \(g(t)\) chosen so the exact solution is \(y(t) = \sin(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(91) * dt                 # 91 samples
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [0, 1, 2, 3]))

print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.2e}")
assert np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))) < 1e-3

# The solution is a piecewise polynomial: evaluate it anywhere in [0, T].
print(f"y(0.5) = {sol(0.5):.6f}  (exact {np.sin(0.5):.6f})")

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: This page collects the rules every solver follows: how the input types select a regime, what the shapes mean, how a solution is evaluated, and why the first-kind solver uses a wider mesh by default.

docs.title: The three equations
docs.text:
All kernels are of convolution type, \(K(t - s)\):

\[\text{VIE-1:}\quad g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\] \[\text{VIE-2:}\quad y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\] \[\text{VIDE:}\quad y'(t) = a(t)\,y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds,\qquad y(0) = y_0\]

They are solved by solve_vie1, solve_vie2 and solve_vide. Every parameter is keyword-only. g=None means g ≡ 0 and a=None means a ≡ 0; solve_vide requires y0.

docs.title: Two input regimes
docs.text:
The types of the data inputs (kernel, g, and for the VIDE a) decide how the problem is posed:

sampled functional Inputs arrays of samples at t = 0, dt, …, (N−1)·dt callables, kernel(u), g(t), a(t) Grid dt (default 1.0); the solver builds a uniform mesh mesh, required: the breakpoints, from 0 to T Node set coll_setting coll_nodes Options of this regime only dt, coll_setting, quadrature, samples_per_interval, kernel_interp_degree mesh, coll_nodes, kernel_singularity, reuse_adaptive_blocks
  • Anything for which callable(x) is true counts as a callable: functions, lambdas, numpy.polynomial.Polynomial, scipy interpolators, numba functions. NumPy arrays are not callable.
  • An option of the other regime is a ValueError that names the regime and why it was chosen. In particular mesh= with arrays and coll_setting= with callables are errors, so you can't silently get a different method from the one you asked for.
  • Mixing the two, e.g. an analytic kernel with sampled g, raises NotImplementedError for now. The combination is reserved for a later release.
import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.linspace(0, 2, 201)
sampled = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=np.cos(t), dt=t[1])
functional = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u), g=np.cos,
                              mesh=np.linspace(0, 2, 41))
print(sampled.regime, functional.regime)          # sampled functional
print(abs(sampled(1.3) - functional(1.3)) < 1e-5)  # True

docs.title: The sampled mesh
docs.text:
In the sampled regime the mesh is uniform, samples_per_interval (Q) samples wide, so its width is h = Q·dt. When N − 1 is not a multiple of Q, the final interval is made longer (up to 2Q samples) to take up the leftover samples. The solution is still returned at every sample, and the convergence order is kept. The kernel needs at least Q + 1 samples.

quadrature allowed Q default Q "product" (default) any positive multiple of divs divs² for VIE-1, divs for VIE-2 and VIDE "collocation" exactly divs² divs²

"product" integrates a piecewise polynomial interpolant of the kernel exactly, uses every sample and accepts any node set. "collocation" uses the interpolatory rule on the nodes. It is a few times faster, but runs only the settings compiled into the extension (divs ≤ 4 in current builds) or, for scalar problems, the numba fallback. See Product integration.

docs.title: Collocation nodes
docs.text:
On each mesh interval the solution is a polynomial, fixed by requiring the equation to hold at p collocation nodes cᵢ ∈ [0, 1] (local coordinates).

Sampled regime: coll_setting. The nodes must sit on samples, so they are given as integers: coll_setting=(divs, choices) means cᵢ = choicesᵢ / divs.

value meaning None VIE-1 (3, [1, 2, 3]); VIE-2 and VIDE (2, [0, 1, 2]) divs every admissible point: (divs, [1, …, divs]) for VIE-1, (divs, [0, …, divs]) otherwise (divs, choices) nodes choices / divs; choices in any order, distinct

divs also fixes the mesh width (above), so settings with the same node positions but different divs are different methods. Floats are rejected, even integer-valued ones, rather than rounded: running a different discretisation silently is worse than an error.

Functional regime: coll_nodes. Any distinct floats in [0, 1] ((0, 1] for VIE-1). The default has the same positions as the sampled default. The classical families come from gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes and lobatto_nodes.

VIE-1 admissibility. A first-kind collocation method converges only if the node set's amplification factor satisfies |ρ| ≤ 1, where

\[\rho = (-1)^p \prod_{i=1}^{p} \frac{1 - c_i}{c_i}\]

for the default discontinuous method (Brunner 2004, Theorem 2.4.2), and the same product over i < p, with c_p = 1, for continuous=True (Theorem 2.4.5). Other node sets are a ValueError. A node set with −1 ≤ ρ < 1 has the method's full order; ρ = +1 converges one order lower and gives an AccuracyWarning.

  • Radau IIA nodes have ρ = 0 and the full order p, which makes them the usual choice for the discontinuous method. They don't suit continuous=True: there |ρ| = p, so that method diverges for every p ≥ 2. The default nodes {1/3, 2/3, 1} work for both methods.
  • Gauss–Legendre nodes are symmetric, so ρ = (−1)ᵖ: odd p keeps the full order, even p loses one.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
The time axis comes first. The component shape cs is () for a scalar problem, (d,) for a system of d equations, and (d, m) for m right-hand sides solved together.

input sampled functional (the callable's return value) kernel (N,) or (N, d, d) scalar or (d, d) g (N,), (N, d) or (N, d, m) scalar, (d,) or (d, m) a (VIDE) (N,) or (N, d, d) scalar or (d, d) y0 scalar, (d,) or (d, m) the same
  • Matrix mode. The problem has m columns exactly when some input has a column axis (g of (N, d, m) or (d, m), or y0 of (d, m)). Inputs without one are shared by all columns, so a (d,) y0 with a matrix g, or a vector g with a (d, m) y0, both work. The columns are independent problems with a common kernel; the kernel's work is shared and the columns may run in parallel threads.
  • Callable kernels are called with one argument u = t − s ≥ 0. A kernel that also accepts a 1-D array of u, returning the stacked values, is detected and used vectorised, which is much faster. For a matrix kernel np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), A) vectorises, np.exp(-u) * A does not.
  • Complex inputs give a complex solution. Integer and float32 inputs are converted to float64.
  • Non-finite data (NaN or inf in an array, or returned by g or a at a collocation time) is a ValueError naming the input and the first bad index. Callable kernels are not checked point by point, since a weakly singular kernel may return inf at u = 0, which the quadrature never samples. A kernel that is non-finite where the quadrature does sample it gives a ValueError suggesting kernel_singularity.
  • A 2-D sampled kernel is rejected; that shape is reserved for non-convolution kernels K(t, s) in a later release.

docs.title: The solution object
docs.text:
Every solver returns a VolterraSolution:

attribute shape meaning t (K,) the grid the problem was posed on: the sample times, or the mesh breakpoints y (K, *cs) the solution at t mesh (M + 1,) the breakpoints node_times, node_values (M, p), (M, p, *cs) the collocation times and the solution there coefficients (M, P, *cs) each interval's polynomial in x = (t − tₙ)/hₙ ∈ [0, 1], monomial, lowest degree first

sol(t) evaluates the piecewise polynomial:

  • a scalar t gives a Python float (or complex) for a scalar problem, and an array of shape cs otherwise; an array t gives (*t.shape, *cs);
  • outside [0, T] the result is NaN. The solution is never extrapolated;
  • sol(sol.t) equals sol.y to rounding.

sol.to_ppoly() gives the same function as a scipy.interpolate.PPoly, for derivatives, antiderivatives, integrals and roots.

docs.title: Values at breakpoints
docs.text:
Collocation solutions of VIE-1 and VIE-2 are in general discontinuous: at an interior breakpoint the polynomials of the two neighbouring intervals give two different one-sided limits. By default sol(t) and sol.y report their mean. sol(t, at_breakpoints="left") or "right" gives either limit. A point within a few ulps of a breakpoint counts as the breakpoint. VIDE solutions, and VIE-1 with continuous=True, are continuous, and the three choices agree to rounding.

The mean is the most accurate choice for most node sets. Measured errors at interior breakpoints, for K(u) = e⁻ᵘ and y = cos t on [0, 4]:

method left right mean VIE-1, default nodes {1/3, 2/3, 1} O(h³) O(h³) O(h⁴) VIE-1, Radau IIA, p = 3 O(h³) O(h³) O(h³), smallest constant VIE-2, default nodes {0, 1/2, 1} O(h⁴) the same (the limits agree to 10⁻¹⁶) the same VIE-2, Gauss–Legendre, p = 3 O(h³) O(h³) O(h⁴) VIE-2, Radau IIA, p = 3 O(h⁵) O(h³) O(h³)

So with VIE-2 and a node set that ends at c_p = 1 (Radau IIA) ask for at_breakpoints="left": the left limit there is the collocation value at the last node, which is superconvergent.

import numpy as np
import voles

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u),
                       g=lambda t: (np.cos(t) - np.sin(t) + np.exp(-t)) / 2,
                       mesh=np.linspace(0, 4, 41), coll_nodes=voles.radau_iia_nodes(3))
inner = sol.mesh[1:-1]                                 # y = cos t
for side in ("left", "mean", "right"):
    err = np.max(np.abs(sol(inner, at_breakpoints=side) - np.cos(inner)))
    print(f"{side:5s} {err:.1e}")
# left  1.4e-10
# mean  8.5e-06
# right 1.7e-05

docs.title: VIE-1: mesh width and noisy data
docs.text:
A first-kind equation is ill-posed: recovering y from g amounts to differentiating g. The collocation method regularises it through the mesh width h, and the error behaves like

\[\lVert y_h - y \rVert \lesssim C_1 h^{m} + C_2 \frac{\varepsilon}{|K(0)|\, h},\]

with m the method's order and ε the noise in g. Shrinking the mesh reduces the first term but amplifies the noise. This is why the sampled VIE-1 default is samples_per_interval = divs² rather than the finest mesh divs, and why samples_per_interval is the parameter to tune on real data. (Noise in the kernel is not amplified this way; it enters as an O(ε) error.) VIE-2 and VIDE are well posed and have no such trade-off, so their default is the finest mesh.

Measured on K(u) = e⁻ᵘ, y = cos t, t ∈ [0, 4] with dt = 10⁻³, the default nodes, and Gaussian noise of standard deviation ε added to g:

ε \ samples_per_interval 3 9 (default) 27 81 243 0 3.8e-10 1.5e-08 2.0e-07 9.3e-06 2.6e-04 10⁻⁶ 8.5e-03 2.4e-03 1.2e-03 3.9e-04 2.8e-04 10⁻⁴ 8.5e-01 2.4e-01 1.2e-01 3.9e-02 1.0e-02

(maximum error over the samples). With exact data the finest mesh wins by six orders of magnitude; with noise of 10⁻⁶ it is the worst choice, and the best mesh is 80 to 240 samples wide. The noise term is about 20 ε / h here. The same noise realisation is used in every row.

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 1e-3
t = np.arange(4001) * dt
g = (np.cos(t) + np.sin(t) - np.exp(-t)) / 2          # y = cos t
noisy = g + 1e-6 * np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(t.size)
noisy[0] = 0.0
for Q in (3, 9, 81):
    sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=noisy, dt=dt, samples_per_interval=Q)
    print(Q, f"{np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.cos(t))):.1e}")

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: Solver calls are thread-safe: concurrent calls from different threads give the same results as serial ones. The compiled code releases the GIL. A matrix-mode solve may use a thread pool of its own, sized by the column count and the number of CPUs.

docs.title: Migration from 0.10
docs.text:
voles 0.11 replaces the six 0.10 solvers with three, solve_vie1, solve_vie2 and solve_vide, which take either arrays or callables. The 0.10 functions still work in 0.11, with a DeprecationWarning, and are removed in 1.0.

Each deprecated call's warning shows the equivalent new call, built from the arguments you passed:

script.py:12: DeprecationWarning: solve_VIE_2() is deprecated since voles 0.11 and
will be removed in 1.0; use voles.solve_vie2(kernel=<array of shape (91,)>,
g=<array of shape (91,)>, dt=0.05, coll_setting=(3, [0, 1, 2, 3])) instead. ...

To find every old call in a code base, run its tests with python -W error::DeprecationWarning (or pytest's -W error::DeprecationWarning). The deprecated functions return exactly what they returned in 0.10: the same values, and the same (values, solution) pair for return_function=True. A few invalid inputs are handled differently; see Behaviour changes in 0.11.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
0.10 0.11 and 1.0 solve_VIE_1, solve_VIE_2, solve_VIDE solve_vie1, solve_vie2, solve_vide, with array inputs function_solve_VIE_1, function_solve_VIE_2, function_solve_VIDE the same three, with callable inputs and mesh= kernel_values=, g_values=, a_values= kernel=, g=, a= soln_init_value= y0= time_step= dt= mesh_breakpoints= mesh= mesh_samples= samples_per_interval= force_continuous=True, soln_init_value=v continuous=True, y0=v arrays: coll_divs=q, coll_choices=[...] coll_setting=(q, [...]) arrays: coll_divs=q alone coll_setting=q arrays: coll_choices=[...] alone coll_setting=(max(choices), [...]) callables: coll_divs=q, coll_choices=[...] coll_nodes=np.array([...]) / q coll_nodes= coll_nodes= (unchanged) show_warnings=False warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.VolesWarning); see Warnings return_function=True, return_polys=True not needed: the solution object is always returned fast_coll_settings_VIE_1 etc. deprecated (they still work in 0.11, with a warning) and not needed: quadrature="product", the default, accepts every setting from voles.solvers import ... from voles import ... optimal_graded_mesh(T=..., M=...) optimal_graded_mesh(t_end=..., n_intervals=...)

kernel_singularity, reuse_adaptive_blocks, quadrature and kernel_interp_degree keep their names. Arrays now go with dt and callables with mesh; an option of the other kind is an error (see Conventions).

docs.title: Return values
docs.text:
Every solver returns a VolterraSolution.

0.10 0.11 and 1.0 array solvers: values, shape (N, ...) sol.y, at the sample times sol.t callable solvers: node values, shape (M, p, ...) sol.node_values, at sol.node_times values, f = ...(return_function=True); f(t) sol(t) f.mesh_breakpoints sol.mesh f[n], iter(f), f.polynomials: numpy.polynomial.Polynomial objects sol.coefficients[n] (local monomial coefficients) or sol.to_ppoly() f._unit (private) sol.coefficients

One value differs: at an interior mesh breakpoint, where a discontinuous solution has two one-sided limits, the 0.10 f(t) returned the right limit. sol(t) returns their mean, which is more accurate for most node sets; sol(t, at_breakpoints="right") gives the 0.10 value. The sampled values (sol.y versus the 0.10 array) were already the mean and are unchanged. See Values at breakpoints.

For derivatives and integrals use to_ppoly():

import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.arange(0, 2.01, 0.01)
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=np.ones_like(t), dt=0.01)
pp = sol.to_ppoly()
print(pp.derivative()(0.5), pp.integrate(0, 1))

docs.title: Before and after
docs.text:
Sampled data:

import numpy as np
import voles

time_step = 0.05
times = np.arange(91) * time_step
kernel = np.exp(-times)
g = np.sin(times) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-times) + np.sin(times) - np.cos(times))

# 0.10
#   values, f = voles.solve_VIE_2(kernel_values=kernel, g_values=g, time_step=time_step,
#                                 coll_divs=3, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2, 3],
#                                 return_function=True)
#   f(0.42)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, dt=time_step, coll_setting=(3, [0, 1, 2, 3]))
values = sol.y
print(sol(0.42), np.sin(0.42))

Callables:

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: np.exp(-u)
g = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))     # y = sin t
mesh = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)

# 0.10
#   node_vals, f = voles.function_solve_VIE_2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
#                                             coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2],
#                                             return_function=True)

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=np.array([0, 1, 2]) / 2)
node_vals = sol.node_values             # (20, 3), as before
print(sol(0.37), np.sin(0.37))

VIE-1, continuous method:

import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.arange(0, 1.001, 0.01)

# 0.10
#   voles.solve_VIE_1(kernel_values=np.ones_like(t), g_values=np.sin(t), time_step=0.01,
#                     force_continuous=True, soln_init_value=1.0)

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.ones_like(t), g=np.sin(t), dt=0.01,
                       continuous=True, y0=1.0)

VIDE:

import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.arange(0, 1.001, 0.01)

# 0.10
#   voles.solve_VIDE(kernel_values=-np.ones_like(t), soln_init_value=1.0, time_step=0.01,
#                    show_warnings=False)

import warnings
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.VolesWarning)
    sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=-np.ones_like(t), y0=1.0, dt=0.01)

docs.title: Behaviour changes in 0.11
docs.text:
These apply to the deprecated 0.10 functions too:

  • Diagnostics are warnings (voles.AccuracyWarning, voles.PerformanceWarning), not printed text; see Warnings.
  • Wrong types raise TypeError, where some raised ValueError or were silently converted: a float where an integer is needed (coll_divs=2.0), a non-bool flag, a non-numeric array.
  • solve_VIDE(soln_init_value=None) is an error; it used to mean 0.
  • NaN or inf in the data is an error, naming the input and the first bad index; it used to propagate into the solution.
  • A VIE-1 soln_init_value without force_continuous=True, which had no effect, warns. In the new API, y0 without continuous=True is a ValueError.

docs.title: Stability policy
docs.text:
From 1.0.0, voles follows semantic versioning on its public API: the names in voles.__all__, their parameters and defaults, and the attributes and methods of VolterraSolution documented in the API reference.

  • Major releases (2.0, …) may remove or incompatibly change public names, parameters, defaults, return types or attributes.
  • Minor releases (1.1, …) may
    • add names, keyword parameters with defaults, attributes and warning conditions;
    • change numerical results, but only as a documented accuracy or robustness improvement named in the changelog;
    • deprecate. A deprecated feature issues a DeprecationWarning for at least one minor release before it is removed in the next major release.
  • Patch releases (1.0.1, …) fix bugs only. A fix may change a result that was wrong.

Not covered:

  • private names (anything starting with _, and every module but voles itself);
  • the text of error and warning messages, and of repr;
  • pickles across minor versions: a VolterraSolution pickled by 1.2 may not load in 1.3;
  • the ABI of the compiled extension;
  • performance, though a regression is treated as a bug;
  • bitwise reproducibility across platforms, builds or BLAS libraries.

Supported Python versions follow the classifiers in pyproject.toml. A Python version past its end of life may be dropped in a minor release.

docs.title: Before 1.0
docs.text: 0.11 is the transition release: it adds the 1.0 API next to the 0.10 one, which is deprecated and still works. 1.0 removes the 0.10 API. See Migration from 0.10.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text:
voles never prints. Every diagnostic is a warning issued with warnings.warn, so the standard warnings machinery controls it.

class base issued for VolesWarning UserWarning the base class of all of them; also a kernel_singularity location outside [0, T] AccuracyWarning VolesWarning the result is less accurate than the method's nominal order: a VIE-1 node set with ρ = 1 (one order lower); VIE-1 with g(0) ≠ 0; VIE-1 with a small or singular K(0) under quadrature="collocation"; a kernel singularity declared on a uniform mesh PerformanceWarning VolesWarning the result is correct but came from a slower path: the numba fallback, or an extension build without a fast path
  • A warning points at the line that called the solver, not at voles' internals, and a solve issues each diagnostic at most once, from the calling thread (never a worker thread of a matrix solve).
  • By Python's default filter, the same warning from the same line is shown once. Use warnings.simplefilter("always", voles.VolesWarning) to see every occurrence.
  • Warnings from other packages pass through unchanged, e.g. scipy's IntegrationWarning from adaptive quadrature of a callable kernel.
  • New warning conditions may be added in a minor release; they are always VolesWarning subclasses.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Silence every voles diagnostic for the rest of the program:

import warnings
import voles

warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.VolesWarning)

or only inside a block, leaving the global state untouched:

import warnings
import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.AccuracyWarning)
    sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=np.cos(t), dt=t[1])   # g(0) = 1

Make accuracy problems fatal, e.g. in a test suite:

import warnings
import numpy as np
import voles

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("error", voles.AccuracyWarning)
    try:
        voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=np.cos(t), dt=t[1])
    except voles.AccuracyWarning as w:
        print("refused:", str(w)[:40])

With pytest, the same is a line in the configuration:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
filterwarnings = ["error::voles.AccuracyWarning"]

From the command line: python -W error::voles.AccuracyWarning script.py.

warnings.catch_warnings changes process-wide state and is not thread-safe; in threaded code set the filters once, at start-up.

docs.title: Deprecation warnings
docs.text: The 0.10 functions issue a DeprecationWarning (not a VolesWarning) naming the equivalent 1.0 call; see Migration from 0.10. Python hides DeprecationWarning by default except in code run as __main__, and pytest shows it.
